docs.title: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization
docs.text:
Welcome, and thank you for joining us. Today you move a real Windows + PostgreSQL VM from VMware onto OpenShift Virtualization, between two clusters and through a disaster-recovery failover, and prove with your own data that nothing was lost. Everything happens in your web browser: this site is all you need.

Begin: Lab 0 Read the student guide

Your instructor gives you one username and password. It opens everything: vCenter, both OpenShift clusters, your Windows VM and its database.

2 · Read the student guide

3 · Do Lab 0

Lab 0 takes about 5 minutes: sign in, open a command line, reach your VM's database.

Stuck, or something not working? Ask your instructor.

They can reset your login, catch you up, or show any step on the big screen. Stuck for five minutes means ask. See Get help for everything else.

docs.text:
• Sign in once and reach vCenter and two OpenShift clusters with the same account
  • Migrate your own Windows + PostgreSQL VM from vSphere to OpenShift Virtualization, cold and warm
  • Go deeper if your class does: disaster recovery, backup and restore, moving between clusters
  • Prove with your own data that nothing was lost, changed or reordered on any move
  • Bonus rounds for early finishers: live migration, snapshot restore, a hostile disaster-recovery failover

docs.title: How the class works
docs.text:
• One VM each: win-pg-s<NN>, a full copy of the instructor's, in your own vCenter folder, at its own address.
  • One namespace each on both clusters, named your class ID. You are admin there.
  • One password everywhere.
  • Only a web browser: nothing to install. Commands run in a terminal inside the OpenShift console.
  • Every step: inject your data → change something → verify it all arrived. Your proof table grows through every demo: it is your evidence at the end.
  • 🧑‍🏫 marks a step only the instructor runs. [verify] marks a step still being proven: if it fails, ask.
  • 🎬 every section has a recording of the same steps in the console: watch it, then do it.

docs.title: Kubernetes in a few ideas
docs.text:
A cluster. A set of machines (nodes) run as one computer. The control plane keeps the desired state; the worker nodes run the workloads, your VMs included. One API serves everything: the web console, oc and automation. OpenShift is Kubernetes plus an installer, a console, security defaults and operators, supported by Red Hat. Each of our two clusters has 4 nodes.

You declare it; controllers make it so. Everything is an object in YAML: what you want (spec) and what is true now (status). Controllers keep comparing the two and act until they match. An operator is a controller with its own object types. Today's: OpenShift Virtualization (VMs), MTV (migrations), ODF (storage), NMState (host networking), ACM (many clusters). You don't run "migrate" as a command: you create a migration Plan, and MTV does the work and reports progress in its status.

A VM is a pod. A pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules. OpenShift Virtualization runs each VM's QEMU/KVM inside a pod (virt-launcher-<vm>): VirtualMachine is the definition, VirtualMachineInstance the running VM. So VMs and containers share one scheduler, network, storage and set of permissions. Live migration is a new pod on another node, with the memory copied across.

Namespaces and RBAC. A namespace groups objects and is where permissions apply, like a vCenter folder with its own permissions. RBAC binds roles (what you may do) to users and groups (who).

Storage. A VM disk is a PersistentVolumeClaim ("I need 10 GiB like this"). A StorageClass says how claims are met, through a CSI driver. Site A runs ODF (Ceph, on the lab's SSDs: snapshots, clones and replication for disaster recovery); site B runs NFS for now.

Networking. Every pod gets an address on the pod network; a Service gives a stable name. NMState builds a bridge for a lab VLAN on each node, and a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) puts a VM's NIC on it. So your migrated VM keeps its address.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You take a real Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM from VMware vSphere onto Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, cold and then warm. You move it between two OpenShift clusters and protect it with OpenShift Data Foundation disaster recovery. At every step you write your own data into the VM's database and prove that none of it was lost, changed or reordered.

This guide is the map. The steps are in the demo guides below.

docs.title: Your login, and what you need
docs.text:
The instructor gives you your login. One student username and one password open everything in this class:

Resource Sign in as vSphere Client (vCenter) and both OpenShift consoles your class ID, with SSO (Entra) Your Windows VM .\student-NN Your VM's PostgreSQL database student_NN

All you need is a web browser. Nothing is installed on your computer. You work in the vSphere Client, the two OpenShift consoles, and your browser terminal: a shell in your own pod in the OpenShift console, where every command in these guides runs. Copy a command here with its copy button; paste it there with right-click → Paste.

Lab 0 walks you through it in about 5 minutes: open the tabs, sign in to vCenter, both OpenShift clusters and PostgreSQL, and see your VM and your access.

💡 A page stuck after a timeout? Sign in again in a private window. Nothing is lost: your VM, your data and your terminal live in the lab, not in the browser.

The zone names (lz1, ocp-lz1, …) change per booking; the guides use them as examples. Your browser terminal already knows your own (type ovedr).

  • Your own VM, win-pg-s<NN>: a full copy of the instructor's, with its own address, in your own vCenter folder. You power it, snapshot it, migrate it and fail it over yourself.
  • Your own namespace on both clusters, named your class ID, where you are admin. Your VM lands there, and your browser terminal lives there.
  • Everything is staged; you do the last step. Each demo's pieces (operators, maps, a migration plan for your VM) are pre-built, and each guide shows how to build them yourself (Lab S). Your task is to review and start.

What Example Where it comes from Class ID (also your project) student-01-0024-012 your sign-in name, the part before @ Your VM win-pg-s01 s + your student number Your VM's address 10.101.23.101 vCenter, step 0.1 Database login student_01 your student number with an underscore, not a hyphen, and not your email address Open in a browser tab Address vCenter https://vcenter0<N>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/ui Site A console https://console-openshift-console.apps.<A>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com Site B console https://console-openshift-console.apps.<B>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com

docs.title: 0.1 Sign in to vCenter, and note your VM's address
docs.text:
1. Open the vCenter tab, choose Launch vSphere Client, then the SSO / Entra sign-in with your class account.
  2. Go to VMs and Templates → datacenter01 → vms → students → <your class ID> and select your VM, win-pg-s<NN> (for example student-03 → win-pg-s03).
  3. On its Summary tab, find IP Addresses. ✍️ Write it down: this is your VM's address (for example 10.101.23.103). You use it in step 0.4, and your VM keeps it after every move.

✅ Your VM is powered on, with three disks (60 GB, 5 GB and 10 GB).

docs.title: 0.2 Sign in to both OpenShift consoles
docs.text:
1. Open the site A console tab and choose Entra (SSO). Your vCenter sign-in carries over.
  2. Do the same in the site B console tab.
  3. In each, Home → Projects shows your own project, named your class ID (for example student-01-0024-012). You are admin there.

docs.title: 0.3 Open a command line
docs.text:
The command line is oc, signed in as you with a token you copy from the console:

  1. In the site A console, open your name (top right) → Copy login command → Display Token.
  2. Copy the line that starts with oc login --token=… --server=….

You can run it in either of two places.

docs.title: Option 1: oc on your own computer (outside this class)
docs.text: If your company allows it, install the oc client yourself: Getting started with the OpenShift CLI (the console's ? → Command Line Tools has the download). Installing it is outside this class's scope: the class needs only your browser. Paste the copied line into your terminal and press Enter.

docs.title: Option 2: a command line inside OpenShift (the class way)
docs.text:
Nothing to install. Use one of:

  • The console's Web Terminal: the >_ icon at the top right of the console opens a terminal already signed in as you. Click Start (leave the project as it is). It has oc; for your VM's database you use the one-line oc exec commands in 0.4.
  • Your class terminal: in your project, Workloads → Pods → sql-client-… → Terminal. It has oc and the class commands (dblogin, mark, sql, verify) ready, and already knows your VM's address and your database login. Sign its oc in: type oclogin and a space, paste the copied line, and press Enter.

⚠ Not the Windows VM's command prompt. Everything in this lab runs in one of the two terminals above.

📋 Copy and paste: paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V, ⌘V on a Mac); copy by selecting the text, then right-click → Copy. [verify: per browser]

docs.title: 0.4 Test: the cluster, then your VM's database
docs.text:
The cluster:

oc whoami            # your class ID, e.g. student-01-0024-012@lab-paragonmicro.com
oc get nodes         # the cluster's nodes, all Ready

Your VM's database, PostgreSQL inside your Windows VM, at your VM's address from 0.1 (the -h below). From oc anywhere (the Web Terminal, or your own computer), each step is one line: oc exec runs it inside your class terminal (sql-client).

⚠ Steps 1–4 are an example. Change two values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID (student-01 on booking 0024-012) your class ID, e.g. student-03-0024-012 (appears in every line, and twice in steps 2 and 4) 10.101.23.101 address of win-pg-s01, the Windows VM running the SQL server your VM's address, from vCenter in 0.1
  1. Sign in to the database, once (enter your class password):
oc exec -it -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- dblogin
  1. Inject a row: the class has started:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-class', 'Lab 0: signed in');"
  1. Read back every row you have posted, oldest first:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
  1. Prove them: no row lost, changed or reordered (one summary line, chain_ok = t):
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

💡 If a step says First sign in to your VM's database … dblogin, your class terminal restarted: do step 1 again.

✅ oc get nodes lists the nodes Ready, the read-back lists your start-class row, and verify shows chain_ok = t.

docs.title: Done
docs.text:
You are signed in to vCenter and both OpenShift clusters, you have a command line, and you reached your own VM's database. Go back to the Student Guide and continue with the next module, Demo 1.

docs.title: Demo 1: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization (cold migration)
docs.text: Version 0.7.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/01-vmware-to-ove-cold.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: You will take your own Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM off VMware vSphere and rehost it on OpenShift Virtualization with the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV). Along the way you will see how OpenShift reproduces what vSphere gave the VM: VLAN-backed port groups become Linux bridges and network attachments, datastores become storage classes, and VMware Tools gives way to virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent. You will also see when to replatform from a Red Hat template instead of rehosting. At every stage you write data and then prove that it arrived intact.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
The CI customization pre-built everything below (see the lab diagram and Toolkit). Every staged piece has a "how it was built" section in Lab S, with the CLI and console steps to build it yourself and links to the Red Hat docs.

Component State when you start How it was built · Red Hat docs Your VM win-pg-s<NN> on vSphere vcenter0<N>, powered on, in your own folder vms/students/<class ID>, at its own address $VM_IP (.100+NN) on port group vm-network (VLAN 22+N). A full clone of the instructor's win-pg-i01: Windows Server 2022, VMware Tools, PostgreSQL 16 with WAL on L: (5 GB) and data on D: (10 GB), the heartbeat writer, the integrity toolkit, and your Windows login .\student-NN (a local administrator on your VM). S.11 Site A (the target) OpenShift Virtualization (ove: cnv, from demo-openshift); NMState bridge br<VLAN> with NAD vmnet<VLAN>; storage on ODF (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization); ACM and cert-manager (base build, the same on both sites). S.2 · S.3 · S.4 · OpenShift Virtualization · NMState [verify link] · ODF MTV on site A the operator, its Migration for Virtualization console menu, provider ovedr-vcenter0<N> linked to vCenter (least-privilege ovedr-mtv@vsphere.local), network maps …-net (pod) and …-net-bridge (your VLAN), storage map …-storage (datastore → ODF). S.5 · S.6 · S.8 · MTV 2.11 · Installing and using MTV [verify link] Your migration plan d1-<your VM> staged, NOT started: cold, your VM → your own namespace ($VMNS, your class ID) on site A, the bridge network map (your VM keeps $VM_IP) and the storage map. It shows Ready in the console. S.12 · Creating and running a migration plan [verify link] Your namespace $VMNS (your class ID) on site A and site B, plus ovedr-app in yours: admin rights for you, Service/<your VM>-sql waiting for your VM to arrive, and your browser terminal sql-client (Toolkit T.1). S.9 · Using RBAC [verify link] Read access for students MTV objects in openshift-mtv (and the right to run plans and migrations), NNCPs, storage classes, ACM clusters. S.9 Site B the same operators, on NFS (nfs-csi); its own staged plan d1b-<your VM>-to-<B> waits for Demo 1b. Not used in this demo. S.12

You do yourself: inspect the VM and the OpenShift side, optionally create your own provider, review your staged plan (and see how it would be built), shut down your VM, and, as the last step, start your plan. Then start the VM on OpenShift, swap VMware Tools for virtio and the guest agent, and prove your data. Your VM keeps its own address, so Toolkit T.4 is not needed.

Pattern at every stage: inject (mark + a line in your file) → change → read (verify + read the file).

Before you start: do Lab 0, then sign your class terminal in on both sites and to your database (Toolkit T.1-T.2: oclogin for site A and site B, then dblogin). It already holds the variables ($ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $WINUSER) and the commands (sql, mark, load, verify, alive, where).

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

docs.title: Networking: from VLAN-backed port group to OpenShift bridge
docs.text:
On vSphere, the VM sits on a port group tagged with a VLAN. On OpenShift, the same VLAN reaches a VM in three layers:

Layer Object What it does Node NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy (NNCP) br<VLAN>-policy builds Linux bridge br<VLAN> on every node, on top of the trunk NIC, tagged with VLAN <VLAN> Namespace NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) vmnet<VLAN> in default lets a VM plug a second NIC into that bridge (Multus) Migration NetworkMap ovedr-vcenter0N-net-bridge tells MTV: port group vm-network → NAD vmnet<VLAN> 
VLAN=$((22 + N))
oc --context site-a get nncp                                                      # br<VLAN>-policy … Available
oc --context site-a get nncp "br$VLAN-policy" -o yaml | sed -n '/desiredState:/,/status:/p'
oc --context site-a get nnce | grep "br$VLAN"                                     # one per node: SuccessfullyConfigured
oc --context site-a -n default get net-attach-def "vmnet$VLAN" -o jsonpath='{.spec.config}' | jq .

✅ The NNCP is Available, every node's enactment is SuccessfullyConfigured, and the NAD's bridge is br<VLAN>. That is the OpenShift twin of the vSphere port group.

The two network maps MTV can use, and the storage map:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get networkmap,storagemap
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get networkmap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-net"        -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}' | jq .
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get networkmap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-net-bridge" -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}' | jq .
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get storagemap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage"    -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}' | jq .
oc --context site-a get storageclass                                              # ODF's virtualization class (site A); site B: nfs-csi
Map Source → destination When to choose it …-net vm-network → pod network the VM gets a cluster address. Clients reach it through Service/$VM-sql. This demo uses it. …-net-bridge vm-network → vmnet<VLAN> the VM stays on its own VLAN and keeps its subnet. Needs the static IP carried over (§1.5, note) …-storage datastore coresan01_data00 → ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization on site A (ODF); nfs-csi on site B where each of the three disks lands. How it was built: Lab S §S.8

📸 01-nncp-available: NNCP list with Available. 📸 01-networkmap-bridge: the bridge network map in the console (Migration for Virtualization → Network maps).

docs.title: Templates: the replatform alternative
docs.text:
Migration is rehosting: the same Windows install, disks and data, now on KVM. Replatforming means building a new VM from a clean, vendor-maintained image, and then moving only the application and data into it.

OpenShift Virtualization ships templates and boot sources for the replatform path:

oc --context site-a get templates -n openshift -l template.kubevirt.io/type=base \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,DISPLAY:'.metadata.annotations.openshift\.io/display-name' | head -20
oc --context site-a get datasources   -n openshift-virtualization-os-images     # rhel8, rhel9, centos-stream9, fedora …
oc --context site-a get dataimportcrons -n openshift-virtualization-os-images   # keeps those images current, automatically
oc --context site-a get datasource rhel9 -n openshift-virtualization-os-images \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}{"\n"}'          # True: a RHEL 9 cloud image is ready to clone

Console: Virtualization → Catalog → Template catalog. The templates with a ✓ Source available badge boot from a Red Hat cloud image in seconds. Windows templates show no source, because Red Hat ships no Windows image: you upload your own golden image.

Rehost (this demo) Replatform What moves the whole VM: OS, disks, data data and application only OS the existing Windows, now with virtio drivers a fresh image from a template (e.g. RHEL 9 + PostgreSQL) Effort low, minutes per VM higher, because the app must be reinstalled Result same machine, new hypervisor a clean, supported, cloud-native-ready VM

📸 01-template-catalog: the template catalog with boot-source badges.

docs.title: 1.4 Link OpenShift to vCenter, and validate the link (10 min)
docs.text:
🎬 1.4 Link OpenShift to vCenter, and validate the link: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01-1-4-link-openshift-vcenter-validate-link.mp4).

The lab already created the link. A Provider of type vsphere named ovedr-vcenter0<N> logs in to vCenter as a least-privilege account (ovedr-mtv@vsphere.local) and pulls an inventory of every VM, network and datastore.

docs.title: Validate the existing link
docs.text:
P=ovedr-vcenter0$N
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "$P" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}  {.message}{"\n"}{end}'
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "$P" -o jsonpath='{.spec.url}{"\n"}'

✅ Ready=True, ConnectionTestSucceeded=True, InventoryCreated=True, and the URL is https://vcenter0<N>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/sdk.

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-vcenter0<N> → Virtual Machines. Find your VM (win-pg-s<NN>) and open its Concerns column. Typical concerns are VMware Tools installed or static IP. Read them now, because they explain §1.5 and §1.6.

📸 01-provider-ready: the provider page with Ready and the VM inventory.

docs.title: Optional: create your own provider [verify: BL-D09]
docs.text:
This shows how the link is made. Use your own name, so that you never overwrite the class provider. The provider belongs in your own namespace $VMNS, where you are admin.

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Providers → Create Provider → vSphere:

Field Value Name ovedr-vcenter-<WINUSER> URL https://vcenter0<N>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/sdk Username / password <ME>@vsphere.local / your class password CA certificate upload the chain from the command below, or tick Skip certificate validation (lab only) VDDK image leave empty (cold migration still works, just slower)

YAML equivalent:

# vCenter's CA chain, taken from its TLS handshake
openssl s_client -connect "$VC:443" -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | awk '/BEGIN CERT/,/END CERT/' > /tmp/vc-chain.pem
read -rsp "class password: " PW; echo
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" create secret generic "ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER" \
  --from-literal=user="$ME@vsphere.local" --from-literal=password="$PW" \
  --from-literal=url="https://$VC/sdk" --from-file=cacert=/tmp/vc-chain.pem \
  --from-literal=insecureSkipVerify=false
unset PW
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" label secret "ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER" \
  createdForProviderType=vsphere createdForResourceType=providers
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER, namespace: $VMNS }
spec:
  type: vsphere
  url: https://$VC/sdk
  secret: { name: ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER, namespace: $VMNS }
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get provider "ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER" -w     # Ctrl-C at Ready

✅ Ready. If it shows ConnectionTestFailed, read the message: x509 means a CA problem, and permission means your vCenter role can log in but cannot read the whole inventory. Either is a useful lesson. Afterwards, clean up: oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" delete provider,secret "ovedr-vcenter-$WINUSER".

docs.title: Review your staged plan
docs.text:
The lab already created your plan, d1-<your VM>, and left it not started. Read it before you run it.

Console: site A → Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d1-<your VM>: source provider, your VM, target namespace your namespace ($VMNS), the bridge network map, the storage map, type Cold, status Ready.

📸 01-staged-plan: your plan's details page, Ready, with the Start button.

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan "d1-$VM" \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.warm}{"  "}{.spec.map.network.name}{"  "}{.spec.map.storage.name}{"  "}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}{"\n"}'
#   false  ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge  ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage  True
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan "d1-$VM" -o yaml | less                 # the whole object

How it was built, and why each field: Lab S §S.12 (the plan) and §S.8 (the maps). Red Hat: Creating and running a migration plan [verify link].

docs.title: Build it yourself (learning path, optional)
docs.text:
To build the plan by hand, give it a different name (e.g. <your class ID>-cold-migration-plan): your VM can be in only one running plan at a time, so start either the staged plan or yours, never both.

Console: site A → Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → Create plan. The wizard has three parts: 1 Basic setup (General · Virtual machines · Network map · Storage map · Migration type), 2 Additional setup, and 3 Review and create.

1 · Basic setup → General:

Field Value Plan name <your class ID>-cold-migration-plan (e.g. student-03-0024-006-cold-migration-plan): unique, and not the staged d1-<your VM> Plan project openshift-mtv (where plans live) Description e.g. My VMware cold migration plan Source provider ovedr-vcenter0<N> Target provider host (this cluster) Target project your namespace ($VMNS, your class ID)

The General step, filled in by the instructor (instructor-01-0024-006, project openshift-mtv, source ovedr-vcenter01, target host, target project instructor-01-0024-006). Use your class ID and namespace. Then Next.

The remaining steps:

Step Choose Virtual machines your VM only (win-pg-s<NN>) Network map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge (vm-network → your VLAN's bridge: keeps your address) Storage map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage Migration type Cold Additional setup leave the defaults Review and create check every value, then Create plan (do not start it yet)

The Virtual machines step. VMs are grouped by vCenter folder: the instructor's win-pg-i01 sits in ovedr, each student's VM in their own folder (student-01-0024-006, …). Expand your folder and tick only your VM. The Concerns badge lists MTV's pre-migration findings for that VM (expand the row to read them); they are warnings, not blockers, for a cold migration.

🎬 The rest of the wizard (network map, storage map, migration type, review) is short and follows the table above; a short screen recording of the whole wizard replaces per-step screenshots (BL-D15).

docs.title: If your plan says "Cannot start" (critical concerns)
docs.text:
Two critical concerns block the start: the plan's maps don't cover your VM's network or its datastore. The two information concerns are fine for a cold migration.

Concern What it means Fix VMNetworksNotMapped (critical) Your VM's NIC is on a vSphere network (vm-network) that the plan's network map has no row for: usually because the wizard made a new, empty map Map vm-network VMStorageNotMapped (critical) Your VM's disks are on a datastore (coresan01_data00) that the plan's storage map has no row for Map coresan01_data00 VM snapshot detected (info) Your VM has a snapshot (the clone source ovedr-golden on win-pg-i01). MTV migrates the VM's current state Nothing to do Disk serial numbers may be truncated (info) disk.EnableUUID=TRUE; SCSI serials are shortened on OpenShift Nothing to do (the guest finds its disks by size and label, not by serial)

Fix in the console: open the plan → Mappings tab → Edit mappings: 1. Network: source vm-network → target your VLAN's bridge default/vmnet<22+N> (keeps your address) or Pod networking. 2. Storage: source coresan01_data00 → target this site's storage class (nfs-csi, or ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization on an ODF site). 3. Save. The concerns clear within a minute, and the status changes from Cannot start to Ready.

📸 01-plan-edit-mappings: the Mappings tab with both rows filled in.

Or, simplest, use the class's maps, which already cover both: build the plan again and at the wizard's Network map and Storage map steps pick Use an existing map: ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge and ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage. These are the maps your staged plan d1-<your VM> uses, and that plan is Ready (Lab S S.8).

Fix from the command line: point the plan at the class's maps, then check the concerns are gone.

PLAN="$VMNS-cold-migration-plan"
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv patch plan "$PLAN" --type merge -p "{\"spec\":{\"map\":{
  \"network\":{\"name\":\"ovedr-vcenter0$N-net-bridge\",\"namespace\":\"openshift-mtv\"},
  \"storage\":{\"name\":\"ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage\",\"namespace\":\"openshift-mtv\"}}}}"
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan "$PLAN" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.category}{"\n"}{end}'   # no Critical left; Ready=True

What a map holds, side by side with the class's own (read-only for you):

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get networkmap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-net-bridge" -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get storagemap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage"    -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}{"\n"}'

YAML equivalent (what the console creates; not started):

oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $VMNS-cold-migration-plan, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: $VMNS
  provider:
    source:      { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host,             namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - name: $VM                # your source VM on vSphere; on OpenShift it keeps the same name
EOF

One VM, one address. Every class VM has its own static address, so the bridge map lets each one keep it on OpenShift: twenty students run twenty plans side by side without colliding. Choose the pod map (…-net) instead and the VM lands on the pod network, where its static address answers nothing: then follow Toolkit T.4.

docs.title: Start your plan (your task: the last step)
docs.text:
Console: your plan → Start → confirm.

📸 01-plan-start: the Start confirmation for d1-<your VM>.

CLI (what the Start button creates):

oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: d1-$VM-1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: d1-$VM, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF

docs.title: Watch the pipeline
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan "d1-$VM" -w                         # Ready → Executing → Succeeded
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get migration "d1-$VM-1" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.vms[*].pipeline[*]}{.name}{"  "}{.phase}{"  "}{.progress.completed}/{.progress.total}{"\n"}{end}'
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc,dv                                       # three volumes appear and fill

The pipeline's phases, in order:

  1. Initialize and PreflightInspection
  2. DiskTransfer: three disks, so three DataVolumes
  3. ImageConversion: virt-v2v installs the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent, and removes VMware specifics
  4. VirtualMachineCreation

Console: Plans → d1-<VM> → the VM row → expand shows the same, with progress bars.

📸 01-plan-pipeline: the plan's per-VM pipeline mid-copy.

✍️ Row 1.3: the migration's start and end times (outage = guest shutdown → first heartbeat on OpenShift).

docs.title: If a step fails: read the logs before you delete anything
docs.text:
A failed cold migration: ImageConversion (virt-v2v) failed, and the error says "See pod logs for details". There is no Cancel on a failed plan, only Delete, and deleting the plan deletes its pods and their logs, so read them first.

The conversion runs in a pod in your target namespace, named <plan>-<vm id>-<suffix>. After a failure it stays there in status Error, with its full log.

Console: Workloads → Pods, project your namespace ($VMNS) → the pod named after your plan → Logs. Or from the plan: Virtual machines → expand your VM → Migration resources → the pod.

Command line:

PLAN="d1-$VM"                                                                   # or your own plan's name
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pods | grep "$PLAN"                          # the conversion pod (Error)
POD=$(oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pods -o name | grep "$PLAN" | head -1)
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" logs "$POD" | grep -E 'virt-v2v: error|error:|HTTP' | sort | uniq -c | tail
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" logs "$POD" > "$PLAN.log"                        # keep the whole log
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get migration -o json | jq -r --arg p "$PLAN" \
  '.items[] | select(.spec.plan.name == $p) | .status.vms[] | .pipeline[] | "\(.name): \(.phase) \(.error.reasons // [] | join("; "))"'

Read the log bottom up: the last virt-v2v: error: line is the verdict, and the repeated lines above it are the cause. For example, HTTP 404 on a …-flat.vmdk URL means MTV could not read the VM's disk from vCenter: the source VM's files moved or were deleted after the plan started. The instructor can collect everything for Red Hat support with MTV's must-gather: oc adm must-gather --image=<mtv-must-gather image for MTV 2.11> -- /usr/bin/targeted --plan=$PLAN [verify: image name and targeted flags, MTV 2.11].

When you're done reading: Actions → Archive keeps the plan's history and removes its running resources, while Delete removes everything. Then fix the cause and start a new plan.

docs.title: Power on in OpenShift
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -o jsonpath='{.spec.runStrategy}{"\n"}'
virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" start "$VM" 2>/dev/null \
  || oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Always"}}'
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" -w                                 # Scheduling → Running

(MTV starts the target if the source was running when the plan began. After a guest shutdown it may stay stopped, which is why this step exists [verify: target power state in this MTV release].)

docs.title: ✅ Check: VMware Tools out, virtio and the QEMU guest agent in
docs.text:
Every migration off vSphere must swap the guest's tools: virt-v2v installs the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent, and VMware Tools must no longer run. Your VM reports its own guest tools at every boot (its heartbeat writer):

tools                                  # platform = not VMware · vmtools = Stopped or absent · qemu_ga = Running · virtio = netkvm,vioscsi…
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}{"\n"}'   # True

✅ qemu_ga is Running, virtio lists the network (netkvm) and disk (vioscsi/viostor) drivers, and vmtools is not Running. In the console, the VM's Overview shows the Guest agent as connected. If vmtools still runs, remove it (Demo 1 §1.6).

docs.title: Your VM keeps its address
docs.text:
The staged plan used the bridge map, so your VM's NIC is on the same VLAN with the same static address, and the helpers keep using $VM_IP. (Only if you built and ran a plan with the pod map: follow Toolkit T.4 with CTX=site-a.)

echo "PGHOST=${PGHOST:-$VM_IP}"         # still your own address
pg_isready -h "${PGHOST:-$VM_IP}" -p 5432

docs.title: The database now lives on OpenShift
docs.text:
where                                   # site-a Running  node=…
alive                                   # postgres_started is NEW (the VM rebooted); staleness < 10 s again
verify                                  # your d1-before and d1-before-migration rows are present, chain_ok = t
mark d1-after-migration "on=OVE site-a"
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, date_trunc('second', gap) AS outage
                  FROM (SELECT id, ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g
                  WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3;"

✅ chain_ok = t, and your two earlier marks are present. ✅ The newest heartbeat gap is the migration's outage.

✍️ Row 1.4: the outage from the gap query, plus the mark id and fingerprint after the move.

docs.title: Your file, read on OpenShift
docs.text:
Console: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → your VM → Console (VNC). Send Ctrl-Alt-Del and log in as .\<WINUSER>:

$f = "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt"

docs.title: 1.6 VMware Tools out, virtio and the QEMU guest agent in (10 min)
docs.text:
🎬 1.6 VMware Tools out, virtio and the QEMU guest agent in: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01-1-6-vmware-tools-out-virtio-qemu-guest.mp4).

On vSphere, VMware Tools provided paravirtual drivers and the guest agent. On OpenShift, virtio-win drivers and the QEMU guest agent do that job. virt-v2v installed them during ImageConversion.

docs.title: From OpenShift
docs.text:
tools                                                                                # the guest's own report (§1.5's check)
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}{"\n"}{end}'          # AgentConnected=True
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" -o jsonpath='{.status.guestOSInfo}' | jq .
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" -o jsonpath='{.status.interfaces}'   | jq .   # IPs reported by the agent
virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" guestosinfo "$VM" 2>/dev/null | jq '.guestAgentVersion, .os.prettyName'

✅ AgentConnected=True, guestOSInfo names Windows Server 2022, and the agent reports the VM's IP. The console's VM Overview shows the same on its Guest agent tile.

docs.title: From inside Windows
docs.text:
Get-Service QEMU-GA, VMTools -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Format-Table Name, Status, StartType
Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Where-Object FriendlyName -match 'VirtIO|Red Hat' |
  Format-Table FriendlyName, Status, Class -AutoSize
pnputil /enum-drivers | Select-String -Context 0,5 'vioscsi|viostor|netkvm|balloon'
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' |
  Where-Object DisplayName -match 'VMware Tools|Virtio|QEMU' | Format-Table DisplayName, DisplayVersion

✅ QEMU-GA is Running. The disks and NIC use Red Hat VirtIO devices. VMTools is gone, or stopped and disabled.

If VMware Tools is still installed, it does nothing on KVM, but remove it: Settings → Apps → VMware Tools → Uninstall, then reboot [verify: whether virt-v2v removed it in this build].

📸 01-virtio-devices: Device Manager showing Red Hat VirtIO storage and network.

docs.title: Update virtio-win and the agent
docs.text:
The replacement for "upgrade VMware Tools" is to mount the virtio-win media and run its installer.

Console: VM → Configuration → Storage → Mount Windows drivers disk ✓, then Restart the VM. Or in YAML:

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type json -p '[
 {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/disks/-",
  "value":{"name":"virtio-win","cdrom":{"bus":"sata"}}},
 {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/volumes/-",
  "value":{"name":"virtio-win","containerDisk":{"image":"registry.redhat.io/container-native-virtualization/virtio-win-rhel9:v4.19"}}}]'
virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" restart "$VM"

[verify: the virtio-win image tag shipped with this cluster: oc get cm -n openshift-cnv virtio-win -o yaml.]

Then, in Windows (as Administrator), run the guest-tools installer from the new CD drive:

$cd = (Get-Volume | Where-Object { $_.DriveType -eq 'CD-ROM' -and (Test-Path "$($_.DriveLetter):\virtio-win-guest-tools.exe") }).DriveLetter
Start-Process "$($cd):\virtio-win-guest-tools.exe" -ArgumentList '/install','/passive','/norestart' -Wait
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' |
  Where-Object DisplayName -match 'Virtio|QEMU' | Format-Table DisplayName, DisplayVersion
Get-Service QEMU-GA

✅ The versions changed (or matched already), and QEMU-GA is Running. Back on the CLI, AgentConnected=True. Remove the drivers disk again in the console (untick it) and restart.

alive && verify                        # the reboots cost heartbeat gaps, never rows

docs.title: Bonus A: live migration between nodes (15 min)
docs.text:
🎬 Bonus A: live migration between nodes: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01-bonus-a-live-migration-nodes.mp4).

Goal: move the running VM from one OpenShift node to another, with no reboot and almost no gap.

A live migration copies the VM's memory to another node while it runs, then switches over in milliseconds. It needs the disks to be reachable from both nodes at once, which means ReadWriteMany (RWX) storage:

  • nfs-csi: RWX filesystem ✅
  • ODF's ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization: RWX block ✅
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="LiveMigratable")].status}  {.status.conditions[?(@.type=="LiveMigratable")].message}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,MODES:.spec.accessModes,SC:.spec.storageClassName
where                                                  # ✍️ the node it is on now
mark d1-bonusA-before

✅ LiveMigratable=True. If it is False, the message names the reason: usually a RWO disk or a mounted CD.

Start the live migration:

virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" migrate "$VM" 2>/dev/null || oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstanceMigration
metadata: { generateName: d1-live-, namespace: $VMNS }
spec: { vmiName: $VM }
EOF

Console: VM → Actions → Migrate → Compute (the wording varies by version).

Watch it:

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmim -w                          # Scheduling → … → Succeeded
where                                                                 # a different node
alive                                                                 # postgres_started UNCHANGED: no reboot
mark d1-bonusA-after
verify
sql -c "SELECT max(gap) FROM (SELECT ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap
                 FROM heartbeat WHERE ts > now() - interval '10 minutes') g;"

✅ New node, same postgres_started, and the largest gap is around the normal 5 s tick (a cold move costs minutes). ✅ chain_ok = t.

📸 01-live-migration: the VM's overview showing the node change, or the vmim watch.

✍️ Row 1.A: from-node → to-node, the max gap, the fingerprint.

docs.title: Bonus B: snapshot, destroy the database, restore from the snapshot's disks (25 min)
docs.text:
🎬 Bonus B: snapshot, destroy the database, restore from the snapshot's disks: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01-bonus-b-snapshot-destroy-database-restore-snapshot-s.mp4).

Goal: take a VM snapshot, delete the database for real, then bring the data back by attaching the snapshot's disks and restarting PostgreSQL.

⚠️ Data and WAL go together. PostgreSQL keeps its data on D: and its write-ahead log on L:. If you restore only D: and keep today's L:, PostgreSQL replays the newer WAL on start, including the DROP DATABASE, and you lose the database again. Restore both disks from the same snapshot. A VM snapshot with the guest agent freezes all disks at the same instant (VSS), so its D: and L: match.

docs.title: Snapshot
docs.text:
mark d1-pre-snapshot "this row must come back"
oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata: { name: $VM-d1-snap, namespace: $VMNS }
spec:
  source: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: $VM }
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmsnapshot "$VM-d1-snap" -w        # Ctrl-C when READYTOUSE=true
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmsnapshot "$VM-d1-snap" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.indications}{"\n"}'                             # ["Online","GuestAgent"]: frozen, consistent

Console: VM → Snapshots → Take snapshot.

Each storage option ships its own VolumeSnapshotClass (ODF's, or nfs-csi-snapclass on NFS; Lab S §S.4); without a class the snapshot stays not ready. Red Hat: Backing up and restoring VMs with snapshots [verify link].

📸 01-snapshot-ready: the Snapshots tab with the snapshot Ready and indications Online, GuestAgent.

Now write a row after the snapshot. It exists only in the live database, so the restore must lose it:

mark d1-after-snapshot "this row must NOT come back"

docs.title: Delete the database
docs.text:
In your VM's console, in an elevated PowerShell (Run as administrator: on your own VM, your .\student-NN login is a local administrator [verify: BL-D10]), stop the heartbeat writer so that it doesn't recreate anything:

Disable-ScheduledTask -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat | Out-Null
Stop-ScheduledTask    -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat

Then drop the database. The bcdr role owns it, and its password is the instructor's, so 🧑‍🏫 ask your instructor to run this from their browser terminal, with your VM's address:

# 🧑‍🏫 instructor (cluster-admin), in their browser terminal: the class pod holds the bcdr owner's password
oc --context site-a -n ovedr-app exec -i deploy/sql-client -- \
  psql -h <student VM_IP> -U bcdr -d postgres -c 'DROP DATABASE bcdr WITH (FORCE);'

Confirm the damage:

verify                 # FATAL: database "bcdr" does not exist. That is the disaster.

📸 01-database-gone: the does not exist error.

docs.title: Shut PostgreSQL down and take the damaged disks offline
docs.text:
Stop-Service postgresql-16
$bad = foreach ($l in 'D','L') { Get-Partition -DriveLetter $l | Get-Disk }
$bad | Format-Table Number, FriendlyName, SerialNumber, @{n='GB';e={[math]::Round($_.Size/1GB)}}
foreach ($l in 'D','L') { Get-Partition -DriveLetter $l | Remove-PartitionAccessPath -AccessPath "$($l):\" }
$bad | ForEach-Object { Set-Disk -Number $_.Number -IsOffline $true }

docs.title: Create volumes from the snapshot's D: and L: and hot-plug them
docs.text:
The snapshot holds one VolumeSnapshot per disk. Pick the 10 Gi (D:) and 5 Gi (L:) ones:

NS=$VMNS; CTX=site-a
CONTENT=$(oc --context $CTX -n $NS get vmsnapshot "$VM-d1-snap" -o jsonpath='{.status.virtualMachineSnapshotContentName}')
oc --context $CTX -n $NS get vmsnapshotcontent "$CONTENT" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.volumeBackups[*]}{.volumeName}{"  "}{.persistentVolumeClaim.metadata.name}{"  "}{.persistentVolumeClaim.spec.resources.requests.storage}{"  "}{.volumeSnapshotName}{"\n"}{end}'

For each of the two rows (10Gi and 5Gi), create a PVC from its VolumeSnapshot. It uses the same class, access mode, volume mode and size as the original:

restore_pvc() {   # restore_pvc <original pvc> <volumesnapshot> <new name>
  oc --context $CTX -n $NS get pvc "$1" -o json | jq --arg s "$2" --arg n "$3" '{
    apiVersion: "v1", kind: "PersistentVolumeClaim",
    metadata: {name: $n, namespace: .metadata.namespace},
    spec: {storageClassName: .spec.storageClassName, accessModes: .spec.accessModes,
           volumeMode: .spec.volumeMode, resources: .spec.resources,
           dataSource: {apiGroup: "snapshot.storage.k8s.io", kind: "VolumeSnapshot", name: $s}}}' \
  | oc --context $CTX apply -f -
}
# fill these four from the snapshot table above: the 10Gi (D:, data) and 5Gi (L:, WAL) PVCs and their VolumeSnapshots
DATA_PVC='<10Gi pvc>'; DATA_SNAP='<its volumesnapshot>'
WAL_PVC='<5Gi pvc>';   WAL_SNAP='<its volumesnapshot>'
restore_pvc "$DATA_PVC" "$DATA_SNAP" "$VM-restored-data"
restore_pvc "$WAL_PVC"  "$WAL_SNAP"  "$VM-restored-wal"
oc --context $CTX -n $NS get pvc "$VM-restored-data" "$VM-restored-wal" -w     # Bound

Hot-plug both into the running VM:

for v in "$VM-restored-data" "$VM-restored-wal"; do
  virtctl --context $CTX -n $NS addvolume "$VM" --volume-name="$v" --serial="${v##*-}" --persist
done
oc --context $CTX -n $NS get vmi "$VM" -o jsonpath='{range .status.volumeStatus[*]}{.name}{"  "}{.phase}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ Both volumes show Ready (hot-plugged on the virtio-SCSI bus) [verify: hot-plug on this cluster, and the vioscsi driver in the guest].

docs.title: Bring the restored disks online as D: and L:, start PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Update-HostStorageCache
Get-Disk | Where-Object IsOffline | Format-Table Number, SerialNumber, @{n='GB';e={[math]::Round($_.Size/1GB)}}, OperationalStatus
# the restored disks have serials "data" and "wal" (from --serial above); match on that, never on disk number
foreach ($m in @(@{Serial='data'; Letter='D'}, @{Serial='wal'; Letter='L'})) {
  $d = Get-Disk | Where-Object { $_.SerialNumber -eq $m.Serial }
  Set-Disk -Number $d.Number -IsOffline   $false
  Set-Disk -Number $d.Number -IsReadOnly  $false
  Get-Partition -DiskNumber $d.Number | Where-Object Type -eq 'Basic' | Set-Partition -NewDriveLetter $m.Letter
}
Get-Volume -DriveLetter D, L | Format-Table DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, Size, HealthStatus
Start-Service postgresql-16
Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat | Out-Null
Start-ScheduledTask  -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat

(The restored disks are copies of the originals, so Windows may first report a signature collision. Bringing the copy online while the originals are offline gives it a new signature. That is expected.)

📸 01-disks-restored: Disk Management, with the restored disks online as D: (pgdata) and L: (pg_wal) and the originals offline.

docs.title: What came back
docs.text:
verify
sql -c "SELECT stage, id, ts FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5;"
alive
mark d1-bonusB-restored

✅ The database exists again, chain_ok = t, and your newest row is d1-pre-snapshot. ✅ d1-after-snapshot is gone. It was written after the snapshot, so it was never in it. This is the recovery point: a restore returns you to the moment of the snapshot, not to the moment of the disaster.

✍️ Row 1.B: the snapshot time, the last surviving mark, and the time the database was back.

docs.title: The other way: restore the whole VM
docs.text:
Swapping disks by hand teaches what a restore really is. In production you would restore the whole VM:

virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" stop "$VM"
oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineRestore
metadata: { name: $VM-d1-restore, namespace: $VMNS }
spec:
  target: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: $VM }
  virtualMachineSnapshotName: $VM-d1-snap
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmrestore "$VM-d1-restore" -w     # COMPLETE=true
virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" start "$VM"

That brings every disk, C: included, back to the snapshot in one step, at the cost of a VM restart.

docs.title: Tidy up after Bonus B
docs.text: The VM now carries two extra (restored) disks, and its original D: and L: are offline. Before the next demo, either restore the whole VM (above), or stop the VM and remove the old volumes in Configuration → Storage [verify: BL-D11, a clean "post-bonus" state for demos 2-4].

docs.title: Bonus C: deploy a new VM from a Red Hat template, on your VLAN, with a data disk (20 min)
docs.text:
🎬 Bonus C: deploy a new VM from a Red Hat template, on your VLAN, with a data disk: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01-bonus-c-deploy-new-vm-red-hat-template.mp4).

Section 1.3 showed the replatform path: rather than moving an old VM, build a new one from a Red Hat-supplied template and boot source, then move the application onto it. Here you do that: a CentOS Stream 9 server in your namespace, attached to your VLAN's bridge (like your migrated VM), plus a data disk. Red Hat: Creating VMs from templates [verify link] · Networking for VMs [verify link] · Storage for VMs [verify link].

docs.title: 1 · Pick the template, then Customize
docs.text:
Console, site A, project = your namespace ($VMNS, top of the page) → Virtualization → Catalog → Template catalog → CentOS Stream 9 VM (centos-stream9-server-small, ✓ Source available).

The template's quick-create panel. Name it <your class ID>-centos9. ⚠ Check Project says your namespace, not default (switch the project at the top of the page first). Click Customize VirtualMachine, not Quick create, so you can change the network and add a disk.

docs.title: 2 · Put the NIC on your VLAN's bridge
docs.text:
Customize → Network interfaces → default → ⋮ Edit. Change Network from Pod networking to your VLAN's bridge vmnet<22+N> (e.g. vmnet23 for lz1), keep Model: virtio, Save.

The template's NIC moved from the pod network to the VLAN bridge vmnet23: the VM is now on the same layer-2 network as the vSphere VMs and your migrated VM.

⚠️ No DHCP on the lab VLANs (BL-D12). On the bridge your VM needs a static address. Set it in Customize → Scripts → Cloud-init → Network data (or the YAML below): 10.101.<22+N>.<150+NN>/24, gateway 10.101.<22+N>.1, DNS 10.101.6.201, 10.101.6.202. Use your NN so no two students collide.

docs.title: 3 · Add a data disk
docs.text:
Customize → Disks → Add disk → Empty disk (blank): name <your class ID>-centos9-data, 10 GiB, Type Disk, Interface VirtIO, StorageClass this site's class (nfs-csi, or ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization on an ODF site). Save.

The Add disk dialog. On nfs-csi, choose Volume Mode: Filesystem (marked Highly recommended) and Access Mode: Shared access (RWX), so the VM can live-migrate (Bonus A); the dialog's defaults (Block, RWO) are flagged Not recommended for this class. On ODF, Block + RWX is the recommended pair.

Then Create VirtualMachine. It boots in under a minute (the boot source is already on the cluster).

docs.title: The same from the command line
docs.text:
Everything in steps 1-3 is one VirtualMachine manifest: centos9-vm-from-template.yaml (also on the Downloads page). It was exported from the console after the steps above, with the cluster-generated fields and the password removed. Each part is commented with the console step it replaces: the root disk cloned from Red Hat's boot source, the blank data disk, the NIC on your VLAN's bridge, and cloud-init for the centos login and your static address. In your browser terminal, it is fetched from the class site, filled in and applied (or paste it into + → Import YAML in the console, with your values in place of each ${…}).

export NAME="$VMNS-centos9" VLAN=$((22 + N)) SC=nfs-csi       # SC: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization on an ODF site
export VIP="10.101.$VLAN.$((150 + 10#${WINUSER#student-}))"   # your static address on the VLAN (no lab DHCP)
read -rsp 'Password for user centos: ' CENTOS_PASSWORD; echo; export CENTOS_PASSWORD   # typed, never in a file
curl -sSf https://paragonmicro-lab.github.io/demo-0024-public/downloads/centos9-vm-from-template.yaml \
  | envsubst | oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f -
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,dv "$NAME" "$NAME-data"                   # DataVolumes clone/create, then the VM runs
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" wait vmi/"$NAME" --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Running --timeout=10m
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$NAME" -o jsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].ipAddresses}{"\n"}'   # your address

docs.title: 4 · Use the data disk, and prove it
docs.text:
Log in on the VM's Console tab: as centos with the password you typed if you used the YAML, or with the user and password the template generated (on the VM's Overview → Details) if you used the console:

lsblk                                   # the 10 GiB disk with no partitions is your data disk (vdc from the YAML, vdb from the console)
DATA=/dev/vdc                           # ← the one lsblk showed
sudo mkfs.xfs "$DATA" && sudo mkdir -p /data && sudo mount "$DATA" /data
echo "$(date -Is) bonus-c $(hostname)" | sudo tee /data/hello.txt
ip -4 addr show                         # your static address on the VLAN
ping -c 2 10.101.<22+N>.1               # the VLAN gateway answers: you are on the bridge, not the pod network

The replatform story: the new server reaches the old one (your migrated Windows VM) directly on the same VLAN. In the CentOS VM:

timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/<your VM_IP>/5432' && echo "PostgreSQL on the migrated VM: reachable from the new VM"

📸 01-template-vm-running: the new VM's Overview, Running, with its VLAN address.

✍️ Row 1.C: the new VM's name, its VLAN address, and that it reached your migrated VM's PostgreSQL port.

docs.title: Demo 1b: VMware to both OpenShift clusters
docs.text: Version 0.5.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/01b-vmware-to-both-sites.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: You migrate one VMware VM to two different OpenShift clusters, first site A and then site B, using the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV) installed on each. You do it twice: once from the command line (you build the Plan and Migration objects) and once in the console, where the lab has staged your site B plan and your task is to review it and start it. That shows the console is a front end to the same objects. At each landing you prove the database arrived intact and that the VMware Tools were replaced by the OpenShift guest agent. CI runs exactly these command-line steps (action=test-migration, automation/test/migrate_both.sh), so a green CI run means they work on this booking.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
Each row points at the Lab S section that shows how it was built (CLI and console), with Red Hat docs.

Prepared by CI Where Check How it was built · docs Your VM win-pg-s<NN> on vSphere, in your folder vms/students/<class ID>, at its own address 10.101.<22+N>.<100+NN>, PostgreSQL WAL on L: and data on D:, validated vSphere lzN alive (Lab 0) S.11 MTV on both sites (migration_tools=both), with its console menu and provider ovedr-vcenter0<N> Ready site A and site B oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider S.5 · S.6 · MTV 2.11 Network maps ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net (pod) and …-net-bridge (the VM's VLAN, NAD vmnet<22+N>) both sites oc -n openshift-mtv get networkmap S.3 · S.8 Storage map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage: datastore → ODF (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization) on site A, NFS (nfs-csi) on site B both sites oc -n openshift-mtv get storagemap S.4 · S.8 Staged plans, not started: d1-<your VM> on site A (Demo 1) and d1b-<your VM>-to-<B> on site B (this demo) both sites oc -n openshift-mtv get plan -l ovedr/vm=$VM S.12 Your namespace $VMNS (admin) with your win-pg-s<NN>-sql Service and your browser terminal sql-client both sites oc -n "$VMNS" get svc,deploy S.9 You can create and run Plans and Migrations, but not change providers, maps or secrets openshift-mtv oc auth can-i create plans.forklift.konveyor.io -n openshift-mtv S.9

Picture: lab diagram. The rule for this demo: only one copy of your VM may run on the VLAN at a time. The bridge map keeps the VM's own address, so a second running copy would collide. Stop each copy before the next move. Because every copy keeps $VM_IP, the helpers work unchanged on both sites, and Toolkit T.4 is not needed.

Already ran Demo 1? Then your VM is already on site A (named $VM in your namespace $VMNS). Skip 1b.2, stop that copy (one copy on the VLAN), power the vSphere original back on, and go straight to 1b.3.

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

docs.title: 1b.1 Inject before you move
docs.text:
🎬 1b.1 Inject before you move: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01b-1b-1-inject-before-move.mp4).

mark d1b-before                        # your row, over the network, to the VM still on vSphere
verify                                 # chain_ok = t
export FP=$(sql -Atc "SELECT fingerprint FROM ovedr_checksum()"); echo "fingerprint before: $FP"

In the VM (vCenter → your VM → Launch Web Console, as .\student-NN):

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d1b-before (vSphere)"

docs.title: 1b.2 To site A, from the command line (you build the plan)
docs.text:
🎬 1b.2 To site A, from the command line (you build the plan): a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01b-1b-2-site-a-command-line-build-plan.mp4).

How each object is built, field by field: Lab S §S.8 and §S.12. Red Hat: Creating and running a migration plan from the CLI [verify link].

CTX=site-a; SLOT=$A; PLAN="d1b-$VM-to-${SLOT}"; PROV="ovedr-vcenter0$N"
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv get provider "$PROV" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}{"\n"}'          # True
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv get networkmap "$PROV-net-bridge" >/dev/null && NET="$PROV-net-bridge" || NET="$PROV-net"
echo "plan=$PLAN network-map=$NET"

oc --context $CTX apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: $VMNS
  provider:
    source:      { name: $PROV, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host,  namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $NET,          namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $PROV-storage, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms: [ { name: $VM } ]
YAML
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv wait plan/$PLAN --for=condition=Ready --timeout=15m       # MTV found your VM

Start it, then watch:

oc --context $CTX apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
YAML
watch -n 20 "oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv get migration $PLAN \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.vms[*].pipeline[*]}{.name}{\"\\t\"}{.phase}{\"\\t\"}{.progress.completed}/{.progress.total}{\"\\n\"}{end}'"
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv wait plan/$PLAN --for=condition=Succeeded --timeout=90m

The pipeline runs Initialize → DiskTransfer (3 disks) → ImageConversion (virt-v2v: virtio drivers in, VMware Tools out) → VirtualMachineCreation. Then start the VM, if MTV left it stopped:

oc --context $CTX -n "$VMNS" patch vm $VM --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Always"}}'   # or: virtctl start $VM
oc --context $CTX -n "$VMNS" wait vmi/$VM --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Running --timeout=15m
oc --context $CTX -n "$VMNS" get vmi $VM \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeName}{"  agent="}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}{"\n"}'

docs.title: Check on site A
docs.text:
alive                                  # heartbeat live again (staleness < 10 s), postgres_started is new
verify                                 # chain_ok = t, your d1b-before row is there
sql -Atc "SELECT fingerprint FROM ovedr_checksum()"            # = $FP: every mark arrived, unchanged
tools                                  # VMware Tools out: qemu_ga Running, virtio drivers, vmtools not Running
mark d1b-after-site-a

In the VM (Virtualization → VirtualMachines → your VM → Console): read the file back, then add a line:

Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt"
Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d1b-after (site A)"

✍️ Row 1b.A: migration minutes, heartbeat gap, chain_ok, fingerprint equal (yes/no).

Stop this copy before the next move (one copy on the VLAN at a time):

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" patch vm $VM --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'   # or: virtctl stop $VM

docs.title: 1b.3 To site B, in the console (your plan is staged: review it, then start it)
docs.text:
🎬 1b.3 To site B, in the console (your plan is staged: review it, then start it): a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/01b-1b-3-site-b-console-plan-staged-review-start.mp4).

MTV powered your source VM off on vSphere. Power it back on first (vCenter → your VM → Power On). MTV copies a VM in the power state it finds it in.

📸 01b-vsphere-power-on: vCenter, your VM powered on again after the site A move.

Site B console (https://console-openshift-console.apps.<B>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com, SSO). The lab staged your plan d1b-<your VM>-to-<B>; it is Ready and not started. Review it screen by screen; the last step, Start, is yours. (To build it yourself instead, use Create plan with the values below and a different name, and start only one of the two.)

  1. Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → your plan d1b-<your VM>-to-<B>. 📸 01b-ui-plans-list: the Plans page on site B, your staged plan Ready, not started.
  2. Source provider ovedr-vcenter0<N>; Virtual machines tab: your VM only. 📸 01b-ui-select-vm: the plan's VM list with your VM.
  3. Target provider host; target namespace your own, <your class ID> ($VMNS). 📸 01b-ui-plan-details: the plan's details: target provider and namespace.
  4. Network map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge (your VM's VLAN, so it keeps its address); storage map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage (datastore → nfs-csi on site B). 📸 01b-ui-maps: both maps on the plan.
  5. Migration type: Cold. Your task: Start → confirm. 📸 01b-ui-plan-ready: the plan page showing Ready, with the Start button.
  6. Watch the pipeline: Initialize → DiskTransfer → ImageConversion → VirtualMachineCreation. 📸 01b-ui-pipeline: the migration in progress, with disk transfer percentages. 📸 01b-ui-succeeded: the plan Succeeded.
  7. Virtualization → VirtualMachines → your VM → Start (if stopped) → Overview: node, IP and guest agent. 📸 01b-ui-vm-overview: your VM Running on site B, with Guest agent: connected.

The same, from the command line (review, then start the staged plan; CI's test runs 1b.2's full build):

CTX=site-b; SLOT=$B; PLAN="d1b-$VM-to-${SLOT}"
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv get plan "$PLAN" \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.map.network.name}{"  "}{.spec.map.storage.name}{"  ready="}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}{"\n"}'
oc --context $CTX apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
YAML
oc --context $CTX -n openshift-mtv wait plan/$PLAN --for=condition=Succeeded --timeout=90m

docs.text: Version 0.6.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/02-vmware-to-ove-warm.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: In this demo you migrate a running VMware VM to OpenShift Virtualization while it keeps serving its database. The only outage is a short cutover. You will turn on vSphere Changed Block Tracking (CBT) for the VM and for each of its disks, and see why MTV needs it to copy only what changed between rounds. You will load the database while the disks pre-copy, cut over, and measure the real downtime from the VM's own heartbeat. Finally, you will prove with your hash-chained rows that every write, including those made during the copy, arrived intact and in order.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
The class CI customization (the customize run that core-web starts after the three environments are built) prepares everything below before you log in. See the lab diagram for how the three environments connect, and Lab S — how this lab was built for the CLI and console steps behind each row.

Pre-built for you Where How it was built · Red Hat docs OpenShift Virtualization (ove: cnv) both clusters (the same operators on both) S.2 · OpenShift Virtualization 4.19 ACM and cert-manager both clusters (base demo-openshift build) S.10 · ACM 2.13 NMState bridges + VLAN NADs (vmnet<VLAN>) both clusters S.3 · Kubernetes NMState [verify link] Storage site A ODF (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization), site B NFS (nfs-csi): one ODF site today, the lab's SSDs fit one S.4 · ODF 4.19 MTV (Migration Toolkit for Virtualization) both tooled sites, with its console menu provider ovedr-vcenter0<N> with network maps (pod + bridge) and storage map, Ready. S.5 · S.6 · S.8 · MTV 2.11 VDDK image on that provider site A prerequisite for warm migration: the lab copies its saved VDDK image into the cluster and sets it here (Lab S §S.15). Without it, MTV can only migrate cold. The demo-prep readiness table says whether this booking has it. S.6 · Creating a VDDK image [verify link] Pre-copy interval shortened to 5 min both tooled sites the MTV default is 60 min between rounds, too slow for a class. S.10 Staged cold plans d1-<VM> / d1b-<VM>-to-<B> both sites for Demos 1 and 1b. Demo 2's warm plan is the one you build here. S.12 Your namespace $VMNS (your class ID, you are admin) with your Service/<VM>-sql and your browser terminal sql-client both clusters your VM lands in your namespace. S.9 Student rights both clusters read MTV objects, bridges, storage classes; create and run your own plans and migrations. S.9 Your own VM, win-pg-s<NN> vSphere vcenter0<N>, in your folder vms/students/<class ID> a full clone of win-pg-i01 at its own address .100+NN: Windows Server 2022 + PostgreSQL 16 (WAL on L:, data on D:), heartbeat writer, the marks toolkit, your Windows login. You can power it, open its console and Edit Settings yourself. S.11

State at the start of this demo: your VM is powered on and writing on vSphere, at its own address $VM_IP. If you ran Demo 1 first, MTV left the vSphere original powered off. Power it back on in vCenter (Actions → Power → Power On; your ovedr-student-vm role allows it on your own VM).

⚠️ One copy on the VLAN at a time. The warm plan uses the bridge map, so the migrated VM keeps $VM_IP. If your Demo 1 copy is still running on OpenShift, stop it first (it holds the same address): oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'.

What you do yourself: enable CBT, build and start the warm plan, cut over, and verify. Your VM keeps its own address on OpenShift, so Toolkit T.4 is not needed.

Before you start: do Lab 0, then sign your class terminal in on both sites and to your database (Toolkit T.1-T.2: oclogin for site A and site B, then dblogin). It already holds the variables ($ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $WINUSER) and the commands (sql, mark, load, verify, alive, where).

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

docs.text: 🎬 2.1 Prerequisites and the starting state: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-1-prerequisites-starting-state.mp4).

docs.title: The name your VM gets on OpenShift

Your staged warm plan d2-<VM> lands your VM on site A, in your namespace, as <VM>-warm. That way it never collides with your Demo 1 copy (<VM>), whether or not that copy still exists.

export TARGET="$VM-warm" PLAN="d2-$VM"

💡 Your chain continues on the vSphere copy. If you ran Demo 1, its OpenShift copy and the vSphere original split at Demo 1's cutover. Rows you wrote on OpenShift in Demo 1 are not on the vSphere original, and that's expected. Your chain on the original carries on from your last pre-migration row.
