Your VM still runs on vSphere, and your browser terminal reaches it at its own address, $VM_IP:

export PGHOST=$VM_IP            # your VM's own address (the terminal's default)
alive                           # staleness < 10 s
mark d2-start                   # ✍️ note the id
verify                          # chain_ok = t

📸 02-start-alive — alive and verify output, with the VM on vSphere.

docs.title: 2.2 Why warm, and why it needs CBT
docs.text:
🎬 2.2 Why warm, and why it needs CBT: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-2-why-warm-why-needs-cbt.mp4).

A cold migration (Demo 1) powers the VM off, copies every block of every disk, then boots it on OpenShift. The outage is the whole copy.

A warm migration works in rounds:

Phase VM state What MTV does Pre-copy 1 running snapshots each disk on vSphere and copies the whole disk to a PVC Pre-copy 2…n running every interval, takes a new snapshot and copies only the blocks changed since the previous one Cutover stopped one last snapshot, copies the last small delta, converts drivers, boots on OpenShift

The question "which blocks changed since the last snapshot?" is answered by vSphere Changed Block Tracking. Without CBT, every round would be a full copy. That's why MTV refuses a warm plan for a VM whose disks don't have CBT enabled.

docs.title: 2.3 Enable Changed Block Tracking
docs.text:
🎬 2.3 Enable Changed Block Tracking: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-3-enable-changed-block-tracking.mp4).

CBT is a per-VM switch (ctkEnabled) plus a per-disk switch for each virtual disk (scsi0:N.ctkEnabled). It takes effect at the next power-on, so turn it on while the VM is off.

docs.title: Leave a mark, then shut your VM down cleanly
docs.text:
mark d2-before-cbt

In your VM's web console (vCenter → <VM> → Launch Web Console, log in as .\<WINUSER>), in PowerShell:

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d2-before-cbt"
Stop-Computer -Force          # a clean guest shutdown of YOUR VM [verify: Users may shut down this server]

Or, from vCenter: Actions → Power → Shut Down Guest OS.

docs.title: Find the exact disk keys first
docs.text:
The VM's three disks sit on one LSI Logic SAS controller, so their keys are scsi0:<unit>. Read the units rather than guessing.

vCenter UI: VM → Edit Settings → Virtual Hardware. Expand each Hard disk and note its Virtual Device Node, for example SCSI controller 0 : SCSI(0:0).

Disk Size Holds Device node (fill in) Hard disk 1 60 GB C: Windows scsi0:__ Hard disk 2 5 GB L: PostgreSQL WAL scsi0:__ Hard disk 3 10 GB D: PostgreSQL data scsi0:__

📸 02-disk-device-nodes — Edit Settings, with the three hard disks' Virtual Device Node expanded.

🧑‍🏫 Instructor alternative (govc):

govc device.info -vm "$VM" 'disk-*' | grep -E 'Name:|Label:|Unit number|Controller|Summary'

docs.title: Set the parameters (VM powered off)
docs.text:
⚠️ Your VM must be shut down. vCenter only accepts these parameters on a powered-off VM, and CBT takes effect at the next power-on. With CBT on, MTV can copy only the blocks that changed since the last pre-copy, which is what makes the warm ("hot") migration in this demo possible.

vCenter UI: your VM → Edit Settings → Advanced Parameters (vSphere 8; older UIs: VM Options → Advanced → Edit Configuration). For each row below, type the Attribute and Value, then click ADD:

Attribute Value ctkEnabled true scsi0:0.ctkEnabled true scsi0:1.ctkEnabled true scsi0:2.ctkEnabled true

(Use the device nodes you found above if they differ from 0, 1 and 2.)

Adding a row: Attribute ctkEnabled, Value true, then ADD. The list's filter (funnel icon) set to ctk shows only the CBT rows.

When all four are added, the list (filtered on ctk) shows them. Click OK:

All four rows set: ctkEnabled for the VM, plus scsi0:0, scsi0:1 and scsi0:2 for its three disks.

🧑‍🏫 Instructor alternative (govc):

govc vm.info "$VM" | grep 'Power state'                                                   # poweredOff
govc vm.change -vm "$VM" \
  -e ctkEnabled=TRUE \
  -e scsi0:0.ctkEnabled=TRUE -e scsi0:1.ctkEnabled=TRUE -e scsi0:2.ctkEnabled=TRUE
govc vm.info -e "$VM" | grep -i ctkEnabled                                                # four rows, TRUE

docs.title: Power your VM back on
docs.text: vCenter: Actions → Power → Power On.

docs.title: Check: CBT is active
docs.text:
When a VM powers on with CBT enabled, vSphere creates a change-tracking file (*-ctk.vmdk) next to each disk.

  • vCenter UI: Storage → coresan01_data00 → Files → ovedr-lz<N>-<VM>/ (each class VM's folder carries its zone, because every zone shares this datastore). There should be one …-ctk.vmdk per disk, three in all.
  • 🧑‍🏫 govc:
govc datastore.ls -ds coresan01_data00 "ovedr-lz$N-$VM/" | grep -- '-ctk.vmdk'            # 3 files

📸 02-ctk-files — the datastore browser listing three -ctk.vmdk files.

Wait for the database to come back, then prove nothing was lost across the shutdown:

until alive 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'beats'; do sleep 10; done
alive                                # postgres_started is new: the VM rebooted
mark d2-cbt-on
verify                               # chain_ok = t — the reboot lost nothing

✍️ Row 2.1: CBT on (yes/no), the number of -ctk.vmdk files, and your d2-cbt-on id.

docs.title: 2.4 Make the database busy
docs.text:
🎬 2.4 Make the database busy: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-4-make-database-busy.mp4).

Warm migration matters when the VM is changing while it copies. Give it something to copy.

docs.title: In the guest
docs.text: Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d2-precopy-started"

docs.title: From your terminal
docs.text:
A burst now, then a small burst every minute in the background, so each pre-copy round has new blocks to ship:

load d2-precopy 500                                            # 500 hash-chained rows, right now
( for i in $(seq 1 30); do load "d2-precopy-$i" 50 >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 60; done ) &
export LOADER=$!                                               # stop it before cutover (2.6)
verify

✍️ Row 2.2: your marks count after the 500-row burst.

docs.title: 2.5 Your warm plan: staged, waiting for CBT
docs.text:
🎬 2.5 Your warm plan: staged, waiting for CBT: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-5-warm-plan-staged-waiting-cbt.mp4).

The lab staged a warm plan for every class VM on both sites: d2-<VM> on site A (and d2b-<VM>-to-<B> on site B, the same plan to the other cluster) (type Warm, target name <VM>-warm, target namespace yours, the class's bridge network map and storage map), not started. How it was built: Lab S §S.12. Red Hat: Warm migration [verify link].

docs.title: Before 2.3: the plan flags CBT (expected)
docs.text:
Open Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d2-<VM> → Virtual machines and expand your VM. Until you enable Changed Block Tracking, MTV flags it, and the plan can't start: this is the point of 2.3. Once your VM has CBT on all four keys and has been powered on again, the concern clears and the plan shows Ready.

📸 02-plan-warm-cbt-concern: your d2-<VM> plan, the VM row expanded, with the CBT concern (before 2.3).

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan "$PLAN" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.category} {.message}{"\n"}{end}'

Expected conditions before 2.3: VMMissingChangedBlockTracking (yours to fix in 2.3). If you also see VDDKInitImageUnavailable, the lab has no VDDK image yet: that one is the instructor's, not yours (BL-B27). Stop and tell them.

✅ After 2.3: Ready=True, and no CBT concern. If the plan still says CBT isn't enabled on a disk, go back to 2.3: a disk is missing its scsi0:N.ctkEnabled, or the VM hasn't been power-cycled since you set it.

docs.title: Build it yourself (learning path, optional)
docs.text:
To see every field, build your own warm plan with a different name, e.g. <your class ID>-warm-migration-plan. Start either the staged d2-<VM> or yours, never both. Console, site A → Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → Create plan, as in Demo 1 (same General step, same class maps), with Migration type: Warm:

Field Value Plan name <your class ID>-warm-migration-plan Source provider / Target provider / Target project ovedr-vcenter0<N> / host / your namespace ($VMNS) VM your <VM> Network map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge (use the existing map; keeps $VM_IP) Storage map ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage (use the existing map) Migration type Warm

Or as YAML:

oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $VMNS-warm-migration-plan, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: true
  targetNamespace: $VMNS
  provider:
    source:      { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host,             namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - name: $VM
      targetName: $TARGET-mine                # [verify: Plan.spec.vms[].targetName in MTV 2.11]
EOF

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
Your task, the last step, once CBT is on and the plan is Ready: console Migration plans → d2-<VM> → Start. Or:

oc --context site-a apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF

docs.title: Check: watch the pre-copies
docs.text:
precopies() { oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get migration "$PLAN" -o json \
  | jq -r '.status.vms[0] | "phase=\(.phase)  precopies=\(.warm.precopies | length)  ok=\(.warm.successes // 0)  failures=\(.warm.failures // 0)  next=\(.warm.nextPrecopyAt // "-")",
           (.warm.precopies[]? | "  #\(.snapshot // "-")  start=\(.start)  end=\(.end // "running")")'; }
precopies
watch -n 30 "oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get migration $PLAN -o jsonpath='{.status.vms[0].phase}{\"  precopies=\"}{.status.vms[0].warm.successes}{\"\n\"}'"

While pre-copies run:

alive                             # STILL writing: the VM is up during pre-copy
mark d2-during-precopy
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc | grep "$TARGET"      # three PVCs filling for your VM

In vCenter, open your VM → Snapshots. MTV creates a snapshot for each round and removes the previous one.

📸 02-precopy-snapshots — the VM's snapshot manager during a pre-copy round. 📸 02-precopy-status — the plan page showing completed pre-copies.

💡 Watch the round sizes. The first pre-copy carries the whole disks. Every round after it carries only the blocks your load loop and the heartbeat changed. That shrink is CBT at work.

✍️ Row 2.3: the number of successful pre-copies before cutover, and how long the first one took versus a later one.

docs.title: 2.6 Cutover: the only downtime
docs.text:
🎬 2.6 Cutover: the only downtime: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-6-cutover-only-downtime.mp4).

Let at least two pre-copies complete, then stop the background load and leave a last mark on vSphere:

kill "$LOADER" 2>/dev/null; wait "$LOADER" 2>/dev/null
mark d2-before-cutover                  # ✍️ note this id: it must survive the cutover
export CUTOVER_AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ); echo "cutover requested at $CUTOVER_AT"

In the guest:

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d2-before-cutover"

docs.title: Cut over now
docs.text:
Console: Plans → d2-<VM> → Cutover → now. Or set the Migration's cutover time:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv patch migration "$PLAN" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"cutover\":\"$CUTOVER_AT\"}}"

MTV then shuts your source VM down, takes one last snapshot, copies the final delta, converts the drivers for KVM, and starts <TARGET> on site A.

precopies                                                            # phase moves past the copy
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get migration "$PLAN" -w        # Ctrl-C at Succeeded

📸 02-cutover-done — the plan showing Succeeded, with the cutover timestamps.

docs.title: 2.7 Validate on OpenShift
docs.text: 🎬 2.7 Validate on OpenShift: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-7-validate-openshift.mp4).

docs.title: Your VM keeps its address
docs.text:
The warm plan used the bridge map, so <TARGET> answers at your own $VM_IP, and the helpers keep working. (Only if you chose the pod map: follow Toolkit T.4 with CTX=site-a and VM=$TARGET.)

VM=$TARGET where                                   # site-a Running, and the node it landed on
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,vmi "$TARGET"
pg_isready -h "${PGHOST:-$VM_IP}" -p 5432

docs.title: Check: every row arrived, in order, unaltered
docs.text:
until alive 2>/dev/null | grep -q beats; do sleep 10; done           # Windows boot + PostgreSQL start
alive                            # writing again, postgres_started = after cutover
verify                           # chain_ok = t; last_stage = d2-before-cutover (or later)
mark d2-after-cutover
verify

✅ chain_ok = t. Every row from d2-start, the 500-row burst, every background round and d2-before-cutover is present and in order. ✅ last_stage before your new mark was d2-before-cutover or a background round written after it. The last pre-copy didn't lose the tail, because the cutover copied it.

docs.title: Check: the real downtime
docs.text:
The heartbeat writer runs every 5 s, so the outage is the gap in it around the cutover:

sql -c "
SELECT ts AS resumed_at, date_trunc('second', gap) AS outage
FROM (SELECT ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g
WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' AND ts > timestamptz '$CUTOVER_AT' - interval '5 minutes'
ORDER BY ts;"

The first gap after $CUTOVER_AT is the cutover. Compare the cutover gap with Demo 1's cold outage (your proof table, row 1.x), which was the whole copy.

📸 02-outage-sql — the gap query result next to Demo 1's.

docs.title: ✅ Check: VMware Tools out, virtio and the QEMU guest agent in
docs.text:
Every migration off vSphere must swap the guest's tools: virt-v2v installs the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent, and VMware Tools must no longer run. Your VM reports its own guest tools at every boot (its heartbeat writer):

tools                                  # platform = not VMware · vmtools = Stopped or absent · qemu_ga = Running · virtio = netkvm,vioscsi…
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$TARGET" -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}{"\n"}'   # True

✅ qemu_ga is Running, virtio lists the network (netkvm) and disk (vioscsi/viostor) drivers, and vmtools is not Running. In the console, the VM's Overview shows the Guest agent as connected. If vmtools still runs, remove it (Demo 1 §1.6).

docs.title: Check: your file came across too
docs.text:
Console, site A → Virtualization → VirtualMachines → <TARGET> → Console. Log in as .\<WINUSER>:

Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt"          # d1 … d2-before-cutover, all there
Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d2-on-ove"
Get-Service QEMU-GA, VMTools -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Format-Table Name, Status   # QEMU-GA Running; VMTools gone or stopped

📸 02-ove-console-file — the OVE VNC console showing your file's lines.

✍️ Row 2.4: cutover downtime (heartbeat gap) versus Demo 1's outage, chain_ok, and the fingerprint.

docs.title: 2.8 Bonus: live-migrate the VM between nodes
docs.text:
🎬 2.8 Bonus: live-migrate the VM between nodes: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/02-2-8-bonus-live-migrate-vm-nodes.mp4).

The VM is on OpenShift now, so moving it to another node in the same cluster doesn't stop it at all. KubeVirt copies its memory while it runs. (This is in-cluster live migration, not MTV.)

docs.title: Is it live-migratable?
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$TARGET" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.message}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -i migrat

✅ LiveMigratable=True. That needs ReadWriteMany disks: true on the NFS class, and on ODF's virtualization class with RWX block. If it says False, read the message (usually the access mode) and tell the instructor [verify].

docs.title: Inject, migrate, verify
docs.text:
mark d2-before-livemig
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$TARGET" -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeName}{"\n"}'     # ✍️ node before
export LM_AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

Console: VirtualMachines → <TARGET> → Actions → Migrate (Compute). Or virtctl:

virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" migrate "$TARGET"

Or as a resource, which is what virtctl creates:

oc --context site-a create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstanceMigration
metadata: { generateName: $TARGET-move-, namespace: $VMNS }
spec: { vmiName: $TARGET }
EOF

Watch it, then prove the data. A live migration keeps the VM's address: on the bridge it stays $VM_IP.

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmim -w                         # Ctrl-C at Succeeded
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$TARGET" -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeName}{"  "}{.status.migrationState.endTimestamp}{"\n"}'
mark d2-after-livemig
verify                                                               # chain_ok = t
sql -c "
SELECT max(gap) AS worst_gap FROM (SELECT ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap
FROM heartbeat WHERE ts > timestamptz '$LM_AT' - interval '1 minute') g;"   # ≈ 5 s: no outage

✅ A different node, chain_ok = t, and the worst heartbeat gap is about the 5 s write interval, so there was no outage. PostgreSQL's postgres_started (from alive) is unchanged, because the database never restarted.

📸 02-livemig-node — the VM's overview page before and after, showing two different nodes.

✍️ Row 2.5: node before → after, the worst heartbeat gap, and chain_ok.

docs.title: Demo 3: OVE → OVE cold migration
docs.text: Version 0.5.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/03-ove-to-ove-cold.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: In this demo you move your VM between two OpenShift clusters: from site A to site B. You will see how Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) links the clusters into one fleet, and how MTV uses an openshift provider, a network map and a storage map to move a VM between them. Because the two sites can use different storage, the move is also a storage migration: the disks are copied from one storage platform to another. As in every demo, you will inject your own rows before the move and prove after it that every one arrived intact.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
The class CI customization (the customize run that core-web starts after the three environments are built) prepares everything below before you log in. See the lab diagram for how the clusters connect, and Lab S — how this lab was built for the CLI and console steps behind each row.

Pre-built for you Where How it was built · Red Hat docs OpenShift Virtualization (ove: cnv) both clusters (the same operators on both) S.2 · OpenShift Virtualization 4.19 ACM (and cert-manager) both clusters (base demo-openshift build). The lab imports site A into site B's hub only when site A is not a hub itself; with ACM on both, each cluster is its own hub today, so 3.2 shows both views [verify: BL-D11, the ACM topology decision] S.10 · ACM 2.13: importing clusters [verify link] NMState bridges + VLAN NADs (vmnet<VLAN>) both clusters same-named NADs on both sites, so VLAN networks map across. S.3 Storage site A ODF (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization), site B NFS (nfs-csi): one ODF site today (SSD limit), so this move is ODF → NFS S.4 · ODF 4.19 MTV on both tooled sites, with its console menu site B (needs migration_tools=both) provider ovedr-ocp-<A-slot> (type openshift, reads site A over api-int with site A's CA), plus its network map and storage map, Ready. S.5 · S.7 · S.8 · MTV 2.11 Your namespace $VMNS (your class ID, you are admin) with your Service/<VM>-sql and your browser terminal sql-client both clusters your VM lands in your namespace on each site; you may create and run your own plans. S.9 Student read access both clusters MTV objects in openshift-mtv, managed clusters on the hub, bridges, storage classes. S.9 Your own VM, win-pg-s<NN> running on site A the end state of Demo 1 (staged plan d1-<VM>), still at its own address $VM_IP on the VLAN bridge. S.11 · S.12

State at the start of this demo: your VM is running on site A in your namespace ($VMNS), and site B has no copy of it yet.

What you do yourself: review ACM and the MTV objects, stop your VM, build and start your plan on site B (this one is not staged: you build it, then the last step is to start it), and verify. Your VM keeps its own address on site B too, so Toolkit T.4 is not needed.

Before you start: do Lab 0, then sign your class terminal in on both sites and to your database (Toolkit T.1-T.2: oclogin for site A and site B, then dblogin). It already holds the variables ($ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $WINUSER) and the commands (sql, mark, load, verify, alive, where).

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

docs.title: 3.2 ACM: link the clusters
docs.text:
🎬 3.2 ACM: link the clusters: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/03-3-2-acm-link-clusters.mp4).

ACM is installed on both clusters by the base demo-openshift build, so each cluster is a hub for itself (local-cluster). The class's intended topology is site B's hub managing site A. The lab's demo-prep step imports site A only when site A is not a hub itself, so on a booking where both are hubs the instructor decides whether to import (below) or to show each hub's own view [verify: BL-D11]. How it was built: Lab S §S.10. Red Hat: ACM 2.13 clusters [verify link].

docs.title: Review the hub and its managed clusters
docs.text:
oc --context site-b get multiclusterhub -A                                  # Phase: Running
oc --context site-b get managedclusters                                     # $A … JOINED=True AVAILABLE=True
oc --context site-b get managedclustersets
oc --context site-b get managedcluster "$A" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}  {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'

On site A, the klusterlet is the agent that reports to the hub:

oc --context site-a get klusterlet                                          # [verify: student read on klusterlets]
oc --context site-a -n open-cluster-management-agent get pods               # klusterlet, work-agent: Running

✅ $A is JOINED=True and AVAILABLE=True on the hub.

📸 03-acm-clusters — site B console, All Clusters → Infrastructure → Clusters, with $A Ready.

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Instructor only: if site A is not imported yet
docs.text:
CI imports site A into site B's hub when site A is not itself a hub (the demo-prep readiness table says which). If it didn't, the instructor imports it once for the whole class [verify: BL-D11, importing a cluster that runs its own hub].

Console (site B, All Clusters perspective): Infrastructure → Clusters → Import cluster. - Name: <A> (for example ocp-lz1) - Cluster set: default - Import mode: Enter your server URL and API token for the existing cluster - Server URL: https://api-int.<A>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com:6443, with an API token from site A (see below)

CLI equivalent [verify]: create the ManagedCluster on the hub, then give the hub an auto-import-secret holding a site A token. The import controller deploys the klusterlet onto site A for you.

# a short-lived token for an account that is cluster-admin on site A (the instructor's)
SITE_A_TOKEN=$(oc --context site-a whoami -t)

oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: ManagedCluster
metadata:
  name: $A
  labels: { cloud: auto-detect, vendor: auto-detect, cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset: default }
spec:
  hubAcceptsClient: true
EOF

oc --context site-b -n "$A" create secret generic auto-import-secret \
  --from-literal=autoImportRetry=5 \
  --from-literal=server="https://api-int.$A.$DOMAIN:6443" \
  --from-literal=token="$SITE_A_TOKEN"
unset SITE_A_TOKEN

oc --context site-b get managedcluster "$A" -w                 # JOINED → True, AVAILABLE → True (Ctrl-C)

⚠️ A whoami -t token belongs to whoever runs it. Only the instructor (cluster-admin on site A) can import. Students only review.

docs.title: Your VM, seen from the hub
docs.text:
Console (site B, All Clusters): Infrastructure → Virtual machines (fleet virtualization), or Search with kind:VirtualMachine name:<VM> [verify: ACM 2.13 fleet virtualization view enabled on the hub].

✅ <VM> shows on cluster $A, namespace <your class ID>, status Running; each classmate's VM shows in their own namespace.

📸 03-acm-vm-view — the hub's virtual machines view, showing the class's VMs on $A.

💡 What ACM gives you here: one place to see both clusters and their VMs, and the trust (managed cluster + klusterlet) that the later DR demo builds on. MTV still does the move. ACM shows you where the VM is; MTV moves it.

docs.title: 3.3 MTV: OVE → OVE provider, network map, storage map
docs.text:
🎬 3.3 MTV: OVE → OVE provider, network map, storage map: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/03-3-3-mtv-ove-ove-provider-network-map.mp4).

The lab's migration fabric already built the OVE → OVE side on each tooled site. On the destination (site B), the objects are:

Object (namespace openshift-mtv, site B) What it is Provider ovedr-ocp-<A-slot> (for example ovedr-ocp-lz1) type openshift. It reads site A through api-int, verified by site A's internal CA, logged in as the service account ovedr-mtv-peer on site A Provider host type openshift: site B itself, the destination NetworkMap ovedr-ocp-<A-slot>-net pod network → pod network, plus every VLAN NAD that exists on both sites with the same name → the same NAD (multus bridge) StorageMap ovedr-ocp-<A-slot>-storage site A's storage class → site B's storage class 
export A_SLOT=${A#ocp-}                                         # ocp-lz1 → lz1
export PPROV=ovedr-ocp-$A_SLOT
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get providers
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get provider "$PPROV" \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.type}  {.spec.url}{"\n"}{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}  {.message}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ type=openshift, url=https://api-int.<A>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com:6443, and Ready=True, ConnectionTestSucceeded=True, InventoryCreated=True.

💡 Why api-int and not api? api.<cluster> serves the public Let's Encrypt certificate. api-int keeps the cluster's internal CA, the one in the provider's secret. A URL and a CA that don't belong together fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. The lab hit exactly that, and fixed it by taking both from the same kubeconfig.

docs.title: Inventory: what site B can see on site A
docs.text:
Console (site B): Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-ocp-<A-slot> → Virtual Machines.

📸 03-mtv-provider-inventory — the provider's VM list, with the class's VMs, each in its student's namespace.

docs.title: The maps
docs.text:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get networkmap "$PPROV-net" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.map[*]}{.source}{"  →  "}{.destination}{"\n"}{end}'
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get storagemap "$PPROV-storage" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.map[*]}{.source.name}{"  →  "}{.destination.storageClass}{"\n"}{end}'
# the two storage classes, side by side
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc -o custom-columns=PVC:.metadata.name,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName,SIZE:.status.capacity.storage | grep -E "PVC|$VM"
oc --context site-b get storageclass

✍️ Row 3.1: the source class (site A) and the destination class (site B), from the storage map.

Booking Site A class Site B class What the copy does ODF on site A (option A) ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization nfs-csi Ceph RBD block → NFS file-backed image: a real storage-platform change (a booking without ODF) nfs-csi nfs-csi same class, different cluster: a copy over the network

💡 How the disks travel. MTV doesn't move the PVCs themselves. For each disk, it creates a DataVolume on site B in the destination class, and CDI (Containerized Data Importer) fills it by reading the source disk on site A over the network. The source PVCs on site A are left untouched. That is what makes a rollback possible (3.6).

📸 03-mtv-maps — site B console, Migration for Virtualization → Network maps / Storage maps, showing the ovedr-ocp-<A-slot> maps.

docs.title: 3.4 Check the destination namespace on site B
docs.text:
🎬 3.4 Check the destination namespace on site B: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/03-3-4-check-destination-namespace-site-b.mp4).

Your VM lands in your own namespace ($VMNS) on site B. CI built the same things there as on site A: your namespace with you as admin, your Service <VM>-sql in it (it selects your VM by name), and your site-B browser terminal sql-client (Lab S §S.9).

oc --context site-b get ns "$VMNS"                                        # your namespace, on site B too
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get deploy/sql-client                      # your browser terminal on site B
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get svc "$VM-sql" -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}'   # vm.kubevirt.io/name=<VM>
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" 2>/dev/null || echo "no $VM on site B yet"   # expected

✅ Your namespace exists on site B, with your sql-client ready, <VM>-sql waiting, and no copy of your VM yet.

docs.title: 3.5 The cold move
docs.text: 🎬 3.5 The cold move: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/03-3-5-cold-move.mp4).

docs.title: Stop your VM on site A
docs.text:
A cold migration copies stopped disks. Stop your VM cleanly first. Windows shuts down and PostgreSQL flushes.

mark d3-last-before-stop "final row on $A"                   # your last row on site A
virtctl --context site-a -n "$VMNS" stop "$VM" 2>/dev/null \
  || oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -w            # STATUS → Stopped (Ctrl-C)
export STOPPED_AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ); echo "stopped at $STOPPED_AT"

(Console, site A: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → <VM> → Actions → Stop.)

✍️ Row 3.2: the time your VM stopped ($STOPPED_AT). The outage starts here.

docs.title: Create your plan on site B
docs.text:
Each student builds a plan for their own VM (students may create and run plans in openshift-mtv: Lab S §S.9). How the provider and maps it uses were built: §S.7 and §S.8. Red Hat: Migrating from an OpenShift Virtualization source [verify link].

Console (site B): Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → Create plan.

Field Value Plan name d3-<VM> Source provider ovedr-ocp-<A-slot> VMs your <VM> (namespace <your class ID>) Target provider host Target namespace your namespace (<your class ID>) Network map ovedr-ocp-<A-slot>-net Storage map ovedr-ocp-<A-slot>-storage Migration type Cold

CLI equivalent:

export PLAN="d3-$VM"
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: $VMNS
  provider:
    source:      { name: $PPROV, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host,   namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $PPROV-net,     namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $PPROV-storage, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - { name: $VM, namespace: $VMNS }
EOF
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get plan "$PLAN" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}  {.message}{"\n"}{end}'   # Ready=True

⚠️ If the plan reports a critical condition, read it before you start. The usual causes are a NAD on site A with no same-named NAD on site B (unmapped network) or a storage class that is not in the map.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
Your task, the last step. Console: Start on the plan. CLI:

oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN-run1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF

docs.title: Check: watch it travel
docs.text:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get migration "$PLAN-run1" -w                # Running → Succeeded (Ctrl-C)
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get plan "$PLAN" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.migration.vms[*].pipeline[*]}{.name}={.phase}  {.progress.completed}/{.progress.total}{"\n"}{end}'
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get dv,pvc | grep -E "NAME|$VM"                  # your disks importing into site B's class
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get pods -l app=containerized-data-importer      # importer pods while copying [verify: label]

📸 03-mtv-progress — your plan's VM pipeline in the site B console, mid-copy (DiskTransfer progressing).

✅ Three DataVolumes on site B for your VM (the C:, L: and D: disks), each Succeeded, in site B's storage class. ✅ The migration reaches Succeeded, and <VM> is created on site B and starts.

✍️ Row 3.3: total disk size copied (sum of your PVC sizes), migration start → end time.

oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get pvc \
  -o custom-columns=PVC:.metadata.name,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName,SIZE:.status.capacity.storage | grep -E "PVC|$VM"

docs.title: 3.6 Validate on site B
docs.text: 🎬 3.6 Validate on site B: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/03-3-6-validate-site-b.mp4).

docs.title: Where is your VM now?
docs.text:
where                                          # site-a -   (stopped)   /   site-b Running  node=…
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get vm,vmi "$VM"

docs.title: Your VM's address on site B
docs.text:
The OVE → OVE network map sends each VLAN NAD on site A to the same-named NAD on site B, so your VM's NIC stays on your VLAN's bridge with the same static address $VM_IP. (Only a VM that was on the pod network gets a new pod IP on site B: then re-read it as in Toolkit T.4, step 5, with CTX=site-b.)

CTX=site-b
echo "PGHOST=${PGHOST:-$VM_IP}"
pg_isready -h "${PGHOST:-$VM_IP}" -p 5432

docs.title: Read and verify: your data
docs.text:
Run the helpers against site B now:

alive                                          # beats resume; postgres_started = the boot on site B
verify                                         # chain_ok = t, marks = row 3.0 + 2 (d3-before, d3-last-before-stop)
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, left(sha,12) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5;"

✅ d3-before and d3-last-before-stop are both there, and chain_ok = t. ✅ The fingerprint from ovedr_checksum matches the one you wrote down. Your VM is yours alone, so no one else's marks are in its database.

docs.title: The outage, measured by the heartbeat
docs.text:
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, date_trunc('second', gap) AS gap
               FROM (SELECT id, ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g
               WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' AND ts > timestamptz '$STOPPED_AT' - interval '1 minute'
               ORDER BY id;"

✍️ Row 3.4: the gap that ends after $STOPPED_AT. That is the Demo 3 outage: stop on A → boot on B.

docs.title: Inject: after the move
docs.text:
mark d3-after "running on $B, storage $(oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get pvc -o json | jq -r --arg vm "$VM" '[.items[] | select(.metadata.name | contains($vm)) | .spec.storageClassName][0]')"
verify

docs.title: The guest tools came along
docs.text:
An OVE → OVE move keeps the VM on KVM, so nothing is converted: the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent from Demo 1 simply run on site B.

tools                                  # qemu_ga Running, virtio drivers, vmtools not Running, as on site A

docs.title: Your file, on the new cluster
docs.text:
Site B console: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → <VM> → Console, log in as .\<WINUSER>:

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d3-after on site B"
Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt"          # d1 … d3-before … d3-after: every line present

📸 03-after-site-b — the site B console, with your file showing the d3-before and d3-after lines.

✅ Every line you wrote on vSphere (Demo 1) and on site A is still there, on site B, on a different storage platform.

docs.title: The source is stopped, not deleted
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM"                          # STATUS Stopped, still defined
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc | grep "$VM"                  # the original disks, untouched

💡 Rollback and cleanup. A cold MTV migration copies. It never deletes the source. Until you clean up, site A still holds a stopped, consistent copy of your VM as of d3-last-before-stop. - Roll back: stop <VM> on site B and start it on site A again. Anything written on B after the move (d3-after) is not on A. That is the trade-off. - Clean up: once you have verified on site B, delete your VM on site A, and its PVCs with it. ⚠️ Never run both copies at once: they are the same VM, with the same database identity.

# cleanup only — after you have verified on site B
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" delete vm "$VM"             # its DataVolumes/PVCs go with it [verify: ownerRefs]

📸 03-source-stopped — the site A console, <VM> Stopped.

docs.text:

docs.title: Demo 4: ODF Regional-DR
docs.text: Version 0.4.1 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/04-odf-regional-dr.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: You will protect running virtual machines with OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) Regional-DR, which replicates their disks asynchronously from site A to site B every 15 minutes. You will prove that a replication cycle really completed, by injecting rows into PostgreSQL and watching them reach the other site. You will move the VMs to site B and home again without losing a single row, and you will see that only the changes travel, not whole disks. In the bonus round you break the replication link, force a failover and measure exactly what an unplanned disaster costs (the RPO).

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
How the two clusters are joined (ACM hub, Submariner with Globalnet, then ODF's MirrorPeer/DRPolicy), what this lab has today and what CI automates: Lab S §S.14. Read it first: this demo depends on all three layers.

The booking's CI customization (the dr-fabric and dr-policy jobs, which run when DR is on) built all of this before class. See the lab diagram, and Lab S — how this lab was built for the CLI and console steps behind the shared pieces.

Pre-built Where How to check How it was built · Red Hat docs ODF on BOTH sites (storage: odf on site A and site B, an operator toggle on the booking) site A, site B oc --context site-X -n openshift-storage get storagecluster → Ready on both S.4 · ODF 4.19 ACM and cert-manager on both clusters (demo-openshift's base build, the same operators on both). DR runs from site B's hub, with site A imported as a managed cluster site B oc --context site-b get managedclusters S.10 · ACM 2.13 [verify: BL-D11] ODF Multicluster Orchestrator and the DR hub operator (Ramen) on the hub, and the DR cluster operator on both sites site B / both §4.2 ODF DR guide Submariner (the network tunnel Ceph mirrors over), the MirrorPeer, both DRClusters both §4.2 ODF DR guide: Regional-DR The 15-minute DRPolicy (sync_interval=15m) site B §4.2 §4.2 Your namespace with your browser terminal sql-client and your VM's Service (<VM>-sql); ovedr-app with the instructor's, on both sites both oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get deploy,svc S.9 Your own VM ($VM, e.g. win-pg-s03) running on site A, on ODF storage (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization), at its own address $VM_IP on the VLAN bridge (Demo 1's staged plan) site A where → site-a Running S.11 · S.12 Your Windows login (.\<WINUSER>) and the PostgreSQL toolkit (marks, ovedr_*) inside your VM your VM verify S.11

What you do yourself: inspect every DR layer, inject and verify data at every stage, read replication status at three levels, and run the moves when you are the driver.

⚠ Capacity, stated plainly. Each ODF cluster takes all 4 scratch SSDs, one on each demosvr host. Today the lab has 4, so it can run one ODF site. Every other demo runs with site A on ODF and site B on NFS. Demo 4 needs a booking with ODF on both sites, which becomes possible when the additional drives are installed. Until then, run this demo from the 📸 screenshots only.

One protection unit for the whole class. Each student's VM lives in that student's own namespace (their class ID), the instructor's in ovedr-app. The default is one DRPC protecting all of them: ovedr-app plus every student namespace [verify: a discovered-app DRPC with several protectedNamespaces]. Every Relocate or Failover moves every student's VM together, so 🧑‍🏫 the driver runs the DR actions, and each of you verifies your own VM. Per-VM protection (one DRPC per student VM, selecting that VM's disks by label) is possible but not built here [verify].

Before you start: do Lab 0, then sign your class terminal in on both sites and to your database (Toolkit T.1-T.2: oclogin for site A and site B, then dblogin). It already holds the variables ($ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $WINUSER) and the commands (sql, mark, load, verify, alive, where).

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

docs.title: 4.0 Point the helpers at your VM
docs.text:
🎬 4.0 Point the helpers at your VM: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/04-4-0-point-helpers-at-vm.mp4).

Use your VM's own address, $VM_IP, for every connection test. Your VM sits on the VLAN bridge (vmnet<VLAN>), which exists with the same name on both sites, so after a Relocate or Failover it comes up with the same address on the other site. (Only a VM on the pod network gets a new pod IP per site: then refresh it with Toolkit T.4 after every move.) Your VM's Service ($VM-sql) also follows the VM between sites.

export PGHOST=$VM_IP                                  # or: export PGHOST=$VM-sql
export DRPC=ovedr-app                                 # the class's one DRPC (ovedr-app + every student namespace)
# the DR state of the class's protected namespace, read from the hub (site B)
drpc() { oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" \
           -o jsonpath='{"phase="}{.status.phase}{"  progression="}{.status.progression}{"  lastSync="}{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}{"  dur="}{.status.lastGroupSyncDuration}{"  bytes="}{.status.lastGroupSyncBytes}{"\n"}'; }
# Ceph's own view of mirroring, on one site (needs rsh into the tools pod: instructor screen if your role cannot)
rbdmirror() { oc --context "$1" -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
                rbd mirror pool status ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool --verbose; }

where; alive
mark d4-start
verify

Regional-DR is built in layers. The lab stages the lower ones (dr-fabric); you inspect each one and see what it is for.

Layer Object (on the hub unless noted) What it does Cluster set ManagedClusterSet, both ManagedClusters ACM knows both sites Network Submariner Broker + add-on on each cluster a tunnel between the clusters' networks, which carries Ceph's mirror traffic Storage peering MirrorPeer (ODF Multicluster Orchestrator) turns on RBD mirroring between the two Ceph clusters and exchanges their keys and S3 stores DR clusters DRCluster ×2 (created by the MirrorPeer) Ramen's view of each site and its S3 store Policy DRPolicy which two clusters pair up, and how often to checkpoint

  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,S3:.spec.s3ProfileName,VALIDATED:'.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Validated")].status'

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: the 15-minute DRPolicy
docs.text:
The user-facing promise of this demo is "a checkpoint every 15 minutes". That is the schedulingInterval.

export POLICY=$A-$B-15m
cat <<YAML | oc --context site-b apply -f -
apiVersion: ramendr.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: DRPolicy
metadata: { name: $POLICY }
spec:
  drClusters: [ $A, $B ]
  schedulingInterval: 15m
  replicationClassSelector: {}
  volumeSnapshotClassSelector: {}
YAML

[verify: dependency] The interval must be one the MirrorPeer offers (spec.schedulingIntervals). The lab's MirrorPeer offers 2m and 5m today, so 15m has to be added to the MirrorPeer for this policy to validate.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
oc --context site-b get drpolicy "$POLICY" \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulingInterval}{"  validated="}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Validated")].status}{"\n"}'
# the per-interval replication classes the MirrorPeer created on each site
for s in site-a site-b; do echo "== $s"; oc --context $s get volumereplicationclass; done

✅ 15m validated=True. ✅ Each site has a VolumeReplicationClass whose schedulingInterval is 15m [verify: class naming, e.g. rbd-volumereplicationclass-…].

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: enrol the VM
docs.text:
The VMs were created by MTV, not by a GitOps application, so they are a discovered application. Protect ovedr-app (the instructor's VM and sql-client) and every student namespace (each student's VM, its disks and its Service), so a move carries everything the class uses.

Console, site B (hub): All Clusters → Data Services → Disaster recovery → Protected applications → Enroll discovered application [verify: BL-T07]: - cluster $A - namespaces ovedr-app and every student-NN-<booking> namespace - policy $POLICY - resources: all in namespace - kube-object capture interval 15m

That creates the Placement and the DRPlacementControl (DRPC) on the hub. As YAML, roughly [verify]:

apiVersion: ramendr.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: DRPlacementControl
metadata: { name: ovedr-app, namespace: openshift-dr-ops }
spec:
  preferredCluster: <A>
  drPolicyRef: { name: <A>-<B>-15m }
  placementRef: { kind: Placement, name: ovedr-app-placement, namespace: openshift-dr-ops }
  protectedNamespaces: [ ovedr-app, student-01-<booking>, student-02-<booking> ]   # one entry per student namespace [verify]
  pvcSelector: {}
  kubeObjectProtection: { captureInterval: 15m, kubeObjectSelector: {} }

docs.title: What "running" looks like, at three levels
docs.text:
drpc                                                           # 1 · Ramen: the last group sync
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplication          # 2 · CSI: one VolumeReplication per disk
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplication \
  -o custom-columns=PVC:.spec.dataSource.name,STATE:.status.state,LASTSYNC:.status.lastSyncTime
rbdmirror site-a                                               # 3 · Ceph: images up+stopped (primary), health OK
rbdmirror site-b                                               #     images up+replaying (secondary)

To see one image's mirror snapshots, which are the checkpoints themselves:

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc | grep "$VM"              # your VM's three disks: pick one
PVC='<one of your VM pvcs>'
IMG=$(oc --context site-a get pv "$(oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc "$PVC" -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')" \
        -o jsonpath='{.spec.csi.volumeAttributes.imageName}')
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd mirror image status "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/$IMG"
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd snap ls --all "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/$IMG" | grep -i mirror

✅ Primary: state: up+stopped, with description showing the last mirror snapshot. Secondary: up+replaying.

docs.title: Inject, then wait for ONE complete sync that contains your row
docs.text:
load d4-busy 200                                 # a burst: the database is busy
mark d4-wait-for-sync                            # the row that must reach site B
T=$(sql -Atc "SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME'")
echo "my row's time: $T"
# poll the hub until a group sync STARTED after your row's time (each sync is a crash-consistent snapshot)
until [ "$(date -d "$(oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o jsonpath='{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}')" +%s 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" \
        -gt "$(date -d "$T" +%s)" ]; do
  printf '%s  waiting… ' "$(date +%T)"; drpc; sleep 60
done
echo "✅ a sync completed after your row"; drpc

The loop uses GNU date -d, which your browser terminal (Linux) has.

💡 With a 15-minute interval this can take up to 15 minutes. That wait is the RPO you are buying. The instructor may use a 5-minute policy in a short session.

✅ lastGroupSyncTime is later than your row, so your d4-wait-for-sync row is now on site B's disks. ✍️ Row 4.4: a typical checkpoint's bytes and dur. Compare them with row 4.3: it should be a small fraction.

📸 04-sync-complete: the drpc line after the loop ends.

docs.title: A snapshot as a local safety net
docs.text:
cat <<YAML | oc --context site-a apply -f -
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata: { name: $VM-d4-pre-move, namespace: $VMNS }
spec:
  source: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: $VM }
YAML
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmsnapshot "$VM-d4-pre-move" -w        # Ctrl-C at readyToUse=true

[verify] snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1 is the served version on OpenShift Virtualization 4.19 (v1alpha1 on older releases).

💡 A snapshot is not DR. It lives on the same Ceph cluster as the VM. It protects against a bad change (Demo 1's bonus round), not against losing the site. Replication is what protects the site.

docs.title: Relocate vs Failover
docs.text:
Relocate (planned) Failover (unplanned) When both sites healthy: maintenance, evacuation, a test the primary is gone or unreachable Order stop the VM on A → final sync → demote A → promote B → start on B promote B from the last completed sync → start on B Data loss none up to one interval (the RPO)

A "clean migration" between sites is a Relocate. The bonus round does a real Failover.

docs.title: 4.8 BONUS: a hostile failover, with a broken replication link
docs.text:
🎬 4.8 BONUS: a hostile failover, with a broken replication link: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/04-4-8-bonus-hostile-failover-broken-replication-link.mp4).

Now the link fails, the business can't wait, and the class forces the VM onto site B from whatever the last completed sync holds. Then it repairs the link and forces the resync back.

docs.title: How to break the link: options
docs.text:
Option What happens Realism Risk Recovery A. Cut the Submariner tunnel (recommended) 🧑‍🏫 Ceph mirror traffic stops. Both clusters stay up, and ACM still talks to both "the WAN link died" low: one label on one node put the label back B. Power off all site-A nodes 🧑‍🏫 (virsh destroy, instructor guide §4.1) site A vanishes entirely "the site burned down" medium: Ceph on A restarts from a crash virsh start; wait for Ceph HEALTH_OK C. Scale down rbd-mirror on site B the secondary stops pulling narrow: a storage fault rook/ocs operators scale it back up unless they are paused too scale the operators back up D. Fence site A (DRCluster spec.clusterFence: Fenced) Metro-DR only. Regional-DR does not fence [verify] — — not used

Recommended: option A. It matches "break the ODF sync link" exactly: replication fails while both sites still run, so the class sees a link failure rather than a site loss. It is reversed with one command. Option B is the scripted disaster in the classic M6 module.

docs.title: Step 1: inject, and note the last sync that got through
docs.text:
mark d4h-before-break
until [ "$(date -d "$(oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o jsonpath='{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}')" +%s)" \
        -gt "$(date -d "$(sql -Atc "SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student='$ME'")" +%s)" ]; do drpc; sleep 60; done
drpc                       # ✍️ lastSync = the last checkpoint that will reach B
sql -Atc "SELECT max(id) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME'"          # ✍️ your last SAFE id

docs.title: Step 2: 🧑‍🏫 break the link (option A) [verify]
docs.text:
# the gateway node(s) on site B carry the label submariner.io/gateway=true; removing it stops the tunnel
GW=$(oc --context site-b get nodes -l submariner.io/gateway=true -o name)
echo "$GW" > /tmp/ovedr-gw-site-b.txt
oc --context site-b label $GW submariner.io/gateway-
oc --context site-b -n submariner-operator get gateways -o wide      # no active gateway / connection error

docs.title: Step 3: keep writing on A. These rows will NOT reach B.
docs.text:
for n in 1 2 3; do mark "d4h-after-break-$n"; sleep 20; done
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 4;"

✍️ Write down these ids and the first 12 characters of each sha. They are the rows you are about to lose.

# in your VM's console on site A
Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d4h written AFTER the link broke"

After one interval, the hub notices that syncs have stopped:

drpc                                                    # lastSync stops advancing
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: Step 4: 🧑‍🏫 force Failover to site B
docs.text:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Failover\",\"failoverCluster\":\"$B\"}}"
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w        # FailingOver → FailedOver

ACM still reaches site A, so Ramen stops the VM there (it becomes the secondary) and starts it on B from the last completed sync.

docs.title: Step 5: measure what was lost (the RPO)
docs.text:
Same address, on site B:

where                                                   # site-b Running
verify
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, left(sha,12) AS sha FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 4;"

What you should see, and why: - The last row present is your last SAFE id from step 1. Every d4h-after-break-* row is missing. - chain_ok is still t. A chain detects rows lost, changed or reordered in the middle. Losing the tail leaves a shorter chain that is still valid. That is why you wrote down your ids: your notes are the evidence of what the failover cost. - Write a new mark on B. Its id may reuse one of the lost ids, because B's sequence continues from the replicated state. Its sha differs from your note, so it is a different row with the same number.

mark d4h-on-b-after-failover
sql -c "SELECT id, stage, left(sha,12) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2;"

# console on site B: the "AFTER the link broke" line is gone, because the disk is from the last sync
Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" -Tail 3

✍️ Row 4.8a: rows lost (count of d4h-after-break-*), RPO (failover time minus the last lastSync), and the outage (heartbeat gap on B).

📸 04-hostile-lost-rows: your noted ids beside B's marks tail.

docs.title: Step 6: 🧑‍🏫 restore the link and force the resync
docs.text:
oc --context site-b label $(cat /tmp/ovedr-gw-site-b.txt) submariner.io/gateway=true
oc --context site-b -n submariner-operator get gateways -o wide       # connected again
drpc                                                                  # progression moves on

If progression stops at WaitOnUserToCleanUp, the stale VM on site A must go before A can become the secondary. That is the instructor's cleanup, in instructor guide §4.3 [verify: BL-T09].

Then watch A's images become secondaries and catch up from the last common snapshot:

rbdmirror site-a          # A: syncing → up+replaying
rbdmirror site-b          # B: up+stopped (primary)

[verify: BL-T09] If an image stays in split-brain or error, Ceph needs an explicit resync of that image on the old primary (A). This copies the whole image, so use it only when Ramen does not recover by itself:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd mirror image resync "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/<image>"

✍️ Row 4.8b: resync bytes and duration. A delta (from the last common checkpoint) proves the DESIGN's claim. A full copy means the hostile path costs one full copy, and the guide says so honestly (DESIGN §6.4).

docs.title: Step 7: 🧑‍🏫 Relocate home, and verify the history
docs.text:
mark d4h-before-home
# wait for one sync after that mark (§4.4 loop, site-b), then:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Relocate\",\"preferredCluster\":\"$A\"}}"
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w
where
verify
sql -c "SELECT id, stage, left(sha,12) AS sha FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' AND stage LIKE 'd4h%' ORDER BY id;"

✅ Present: d4h-before-break, d4h-on-b-after-failover and d4h-before-home. ✅ Missing: every d4h-after-break-*. These were written only on A after the link broke, then discarded when A was resynced from B. That is exactly the data the hostile failover cost. ✅ chain_ok = t on A. The chain continues from the last safe row, through B, and home.

Row Stage Bytes Duration Rows lost Notes 4.8a forced Failover A ✗ → B — RPO = 4.8b resync after the link returns — delta or full? 4.8c Relocate home 0

📸 04-hostile-home: the final d4h% query on site A.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Regional-DR asynchronous replication between two clusters. RPO is greater than 0, at most one schedulingInterval MirrorPeer ODF Multicluster Orchestrator's pairing of two Ceph clusters, which turns on RBD mirroring DRPolicy the two clusters, and the checkpoint interval (here 15m) DRPC DRPlacementControl: the DR state of one protected workload, and where you ask for Relocate or Failover VRG VolumeReplicationGroup: the per-cluster agent that makes the workload's disks primary or secondary Relocate planned move: final sync, zero loss Failover forced move from the last completed sync: loss up to one interval RPO / RTO how much data you can lose / how long you are down

docs.title: Demo 5 (bonus): Back up and restore your VM with OADP
docs.text:
Version 0.2.1 · framework · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/05-oadp-vm-backup.md

🚧 Bonus, framework. OADP is now built by the lab when a class books it (option backup: oadp, the default for this class). The commands below are unproven [verify] until a booking has run them. Ask your instructor whether your lab has OADP before you start.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Disaster recovery (Demo 4) keeps a running copy on another site. A backup is different: a point-in-time copy you can restore after a mistake, a bad change or a ransomware event, even when every replica has the damage too. You will back up your whole namespace with OADP (the OpenShift API for Data Protection, Red Hat's Velero-based operator): the VirtualMachine, its disks and its Service. Then you delete it all, restore it, and prove with your own rows that the restored VM holds exactly the data it had at backup time.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
Where What is pre-built (planned) How it is built Both sites (demo-openshift, backup: oadp) the OADP operator (1.5) in openshift-adp, a DataProtectionApplication with the openshift, aws, kubevirt and csi plugins, the node agent and the Data Mover (disk snapshots copied off the cluster), and non-admin backups: you back up and restore your own namespace yourself OADP [verify link] Both sites a backup location on the lab's object store (MinIO, outside the clusters), one bucket per cluster and a folder per booking: backups outlive the cluster Backup locations [verify link] You your VM running on site A (after Demo 1), in your namespace —

You do yourself: inject data, request a backup of your namespace, delete your VM, restore it, and verify.

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal (Toolkit T.1), signed in on site A, with dblogin done. powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console.

docs.title: 5.1 What a VM backup contains
docs.text:
🎬 5.1 What a VM backup contains: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/05-5-1-what-vm-backup-contains.mp4).

A backup of your namespace captures its objects (the VirtualMachine, its DataVolumes and PVCs, the Service) and its data: each disk is snapshotted, and the Data Mover copies the snapshot to object storage, so the backup survives even if the cluster's storage is lost. A running Windows VM is backed up crash-consistent unless the guest agent freezes it first: PostgreSQL recovers from that like from a power cut, and your hash chain proves it.

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,dv,pvc,svc               # what your backup will contain
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackupstoragelocations.oadp.openshift.io 2>/dev/null || echo "(the class's location is the default one)"   # [verify]

💡 Use full resource names here. On these clusters oc get backup finds ODF's database-backup type and oc get restore finds ACM's, not OADP's. Several operators define a "backup" or "restore". Always write the full name, for example nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io or backups.velero.io.

docs.title: 5.2 Inject before the backup
docs.text:
🎬 5.2 Inject before the backup: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/05-5-2-inject-before-backup.mp4).

alive                              # your VM is writing
mark d5-in-backup                  # ✍️ note the id: this row MUST come back
verify                             # chain_ok = t

In the VM's console (PowerShell):

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d5-in-backup"

docs.title: 5.3 Back up your namespace
docs.text:
🎬 5.3 Back up your namespace: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/05-5-3-back-up-namespace.mp4).

You create a NonAdminBackup in your own namespace; OADP turns it into a backup of that namespace only. [verify: the NonAdminBackup fields and the student rights on OADP 1.5 (demo-openshift reports what the operator grants)]

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: oadp.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: NonAdminBackup
metadata: { name: d5 }
spec:
  backupSpec:
    snapshotMoveData: true        # the Data Mover: your disks' data leaves the cluster's storage
    ttl: 24h0m0s
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io d5 -w            # Ctrl-C when its phase is Created and the backup Completed
mark d5-after-backup               # this row is NOT in the backup: it must be gone after the restore

Console: your project → Operators → Installed Operators → OADP → NonAdminBackup → Create.

✍️ Row 5.3: the backup's duration and size (oc -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io d5 -o yaml, under status).

docs.title: 5.4 Lose it: delete your VM
docs.text:
🎬 5.4 Lose it: delete your VM: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/05-5-4-lose-delete-vm.mp4).

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" delete vm "$VM"                     # the VM and its disks are gone
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,pvc                          # nothing left of your VM
alive                                                              # fails: that is the disaster

docs.title: 5.5 Restore, and prove the data
docs.text:
🎬 5.5 Restore, and prove the data: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/05-5-5-restore-prove-data.mp4).

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: oadp.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: NonAdminRestore
metadata: { name: d5 }
spec:
  restoreSpec:
    backupName: d5                # your NonAdminBackup   [verify]
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminrestores.oadp.openshift.io d5 -w           # Ctrl-C when the restore Completed
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -w                      # Running again
until alive >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 10; done; alive              # Windows booted, PostgreSQL recovered
verify                                                             # chain_ok = t
sql -c "SELECT stage FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' AND stage LIKE 'd5-%' ORDER BY id;"

✅ d5-in-backup is back and chain_ok = t. d5-after-backup is gone: it was written after the backup, which is exactly what a restore means. Your file in the VM ends at d5-in-backup too.

✍️ Row 5.5: the restore's duration, chain_ok, and which of your rows came back.

docs.title: Thank you
docs.text:
You protected a VM the way a platform team protects any application on OpenShift: one backup of the namespace, its objects and its disks, restored in place. To go deeper:

  • Backing up and restoring virtual machines (OpenShift Virtualization 4.19) [verify link]
  • Velero, the upstream project

docs.title: Lab S: How this lab was built
docs.text: Version 0.5.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/setup-how-the-lab-is-built.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Before your class started, a CI pipeline built three environments and then customized them: operators, networks, storage, migration providers and maps, a namespace with a database client, one Windows + PostgreSQL VM per student, and a staged migration plan for each VM. This guide walks through every one of those pieces in the order CI builds them. For each piece you see what was built, how to check it, how to build it yourself from the command line, and how to do the same in the console, with links to the Red Hat documentation that describes it. The demo guides only ask you to do the last step yourself (start your migration). This guide is how you would do everything before it.

docs.title: How the lab is set up
docs.text:
Built by What Where demo-vmware (core-web dispatches it) vCenter vcenter0<N>, 4 nested ESXi hosts, the shared NFS datastore coresan01_data00, port group vm-network on VLAN 22+N, your vCenter folder vms/students/<your ID> vSphere lzN demo-openshift (core-web dispatches it, twice) OpenShift 4.19, OpenShift Virtualization (ove: cnv), ACM and cert-manager, NMState bridges + NADs per VLAN, nfs-csi storage; ODF on site A only site A <A> and site B <B> this demo's CI (customize, sections S.5–S.12) MTV, providers, maps, the class namespace, the class VMs, demo prep, the staged plans all three you start your own migration plan (Demo 1 / 1b), then everything in the demo guides

Picture: lab diagram. Every command below uses your class terminal's variables ($A, $B, $N, $VM, $DOMAIN; Toolkit T.1) and the contexts site-a / site-b. Most "do it yourself" steps need cluster-admin. In class you only read these objects; the instructor (or a cluster you own) can run the build steps.

export VLAN=$((22 + N))                 # the vSphere zone's VLAN: also the bridge your migrated VM can join

docs.title: S.1 The three environments, and what both clusters should look like
docs.text:
What CI built: core-web booked one vSphere zone and two OpenShift clusters together. Both clusters are built from the same member selections (ove: cnv, ACM, cert-manager), so they carry the same operators. The one difference is storage: the lab has four scratch SSDs, enough for one ODF cluster, so site A runs ODF and site B uses NFS (nfs-csi). The healthcheck compares the two sites' operators and reports any difference (ODF excluded).

Check:

for s in site-a site-b; do echo "== $s"; oc --context $s get csv -A --no-headers \
  | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/\.v\{0,1\}[0-9].*$//' | sort -u; done
oc --context site-a get storageclass; oc --context site-b get storageclass

Console: Operators → Installed Operators, project All Projects, on each site. 📸 S-operators-site-a · 📸 S-operators-site-b: the two installed-operator lists side by side.

Red Hat docs: - OpenShift Container Platform 4.19 documentation - Operators: understanding OLM and installed operators - About OpenShift Virtualization

docs.title: S.2 OpenShift Virtualization (built by demo-openshift)
docs.text:
What was built: the OpenShift Virtualization operator (kubevirt-hyperconverged) in openshift-cnv, and its HyperConverged resource kubevirt-hyperconverged. That resource deploys KubeVirt, CDI (the disk importer), the templates and the boot sources.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-cnv get hyperconverged kubevirt-hyperconverged \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Available")].status}{"\n"}'      # True
oc --context site-a -n openshift-cnv get csv | grep -i kubevirt

Do it yourself (CLI):

oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: { name: openshift-cnv }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata: { name: kubevirt-hyperconverged-group, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: { targetNamespaces: [ openshift-cnv ] }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata: { name: hco-operatorhub, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: { source: redhat-operators, sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace, name: kubevirt-hyperconverged, channel: stable }
YAML
# once the CSV says Succeeded:
oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: hco.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: HyperConverged
metadata: { name: kubevirt-hyperconverged, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: {}
YAML

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → search OpenShift Virtualization → Install (namespace openshift-cnv). 📸 S-cnv-operatorhub 2. Installed Operators → OpenShift Virtualization → Create HyperConverged → Create. 📸 S-cnv-hyperconverged 3. A Virtualization menu appears in the left navigation. 📸 S-cnv-menu

Red Hat docs: - Installing OpenShift Virtualization - Preparing your cluster for OpenShift Virtualization [verify link] - OpenShift Virtualization architecture [verify link]

docs.title: S.3 Networking: VLANs to bridges to network attachments
docs.text:
What was built (demo-openshift): the Kubernetes NMState operator, and on every node a Linux bridge br<VLAN> on the trunk NIC for each lab VLAN. Each bridge is a NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy (NNCP) named br<VLAN>-policy. In default there is a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) vmnet<VLAN> that lets a VM plug into that bridge. The VLAN is the same one the vSphere port group vm-network uses, so a migrated VM can keep its address.

vSphere OpenShift port group vm-network, VLAN 22+N NNCP br<22+N>-policy → bridge br<22+N> → NAD default/vmnet<22+N>

Check:

oc --context site-a get nncp                                                   # br<VLAN>-policy … Available
oc --context site-a get nncp "br${VLAN}-policy" -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Available")].status}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n default get net-attach-def "vmnet${VLAN}" -o jsonpath='{.spec.config}{"\n"}' | jq .

Do it yourself (CLI): install Kubernetes NMState Operator from OperatorHub, create its NMState instance, then:

TRUNK='<trunk NIC on the nodes, e.g. ens224>'          # [verify] the trunk interface name on your nodes
oc apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata: { name: br${VLAN}-policy }
spec:
  desiredState:
    interfaces:
      - name: ${TRUNK}.${VLAN}
        type: vlan
        state: up
        vlan: { base-iface: ${TRUNK}, id: ${VLAN} }
      - name: br${VLAN}
        type: linux-bridge
        state: up
        ipv4: { enabled: false }
        bridge: { options: { stp: { enabled: false } }, port: [ { name: ${TRUNK}.${VLAN} } ] }
---
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata: { name: vmnet${VLAN}, namespace: default }
spec:
  config: '{"cniVersion":"0.3.1","name":"vmnet${VLAN}","type":"bridge","bridge":"br${VLAN}","macspoofchk":true}'
YAML

Console: 1. Networking → NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy → Create (form or YAML), as above. 📸 S-nncp-create 2. Wait for Available on every node. 📸 S-nncp-available 3. Networking → NetworkAttachmentDefinitions → Create in default: type Linux bridge, bridge name br<VLAN>. 📸 S-nad-create

Red Hat docs: - Kubernetes NMState operator [verify link] - Connecting a VM to a Linux bridge network [verify link] - Multiple networks: NetworkAttachmentDefinition [verify link]

docs.title: S.4 Storage: whatever the booking chose, and snapshot classes
docs.text:
Storage is not this demo's choice. demo-openshift deploys each cluster's storage from its storage option (na = NFS, odf; other storage providers such as Portworx are forks of this class, BL-D25) and marks the class VMs belong on. CI's customize only reads that class (the storageclass.kubevirt.io/is-default-virt-class one, else the cluster default) and proves a test claim binds before any VM lands there. The demos work the same on any of them: they are about migration and BCDR.

# the class your VMs land on, per site (what CI's sc_live reads)
for s in site-a site-b; do
  oc --context $s get sc -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.metadata.annotations.storageclass\.kubevirt\.io/is-default-virt-class=="true")]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'
done

What this booking's build has today: - Site A: OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF), Ceph on the four scratch SSDs. VMs use the storage class ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (block, RWX, so live migration works). Built by demo-openshift (storage: odf); core-web reserves the SSDs for the booking. - Site B: nfs-csi on the lab NFS server (demo-openshift's default). - Snapshot classes come with the storage, from demo-openshift: nfs-csi-snapclass (driver nfs.csi.k8s.io) and ODF's own. Demo 1's snapshot bonus needs one. CI's demo-prep only reports a VM storage driver without one.

Check:

oc --context site-a get storageclass ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage get storagecluster      # Ready
oc --context site-b get storageclass nfs-csi
for s in site-a site-b; do oc --context $s get volumesnapshotclass; done

Do it yourself (CLI): a snapshot class for a driver that has none (what demo-openshift creates for NFS):

oc --context site-b apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata: { name: nfs-csi-snapclass }
driver: nfs.csi.k8s.io
deletionPolicy: Delete
YAML

ODF itself: install the OpenShift Data Foundation operator, label the storage nodes, and create a StorageSystem / StorageCluster on the local SSDs (the Local Storage operator discovers them).

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → OpenShift Data Foundation → Install. 📸 S-odf-install 2. Storage → Data Foundation → Create StorageSystem → Create a new StorageClass using local storage devices. 📸 S-odf-storagesystem 3. Storage → StorageClasses: see ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (site A) and nfs-csi (site B). 📸 S-storageclasses 4. Storage → VolumeSnapshotClasses → Create. 📸 S-snapclass
