docs.title: S.5 The Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV) operator
docs.text:
Who built it: the booking's migration_tools decides which sites get MTV (both: site A and site B; site-a: site B is left bare so students install MTV there). On those sites demo-openshift installs it (ove: cnv-mtv), and CI (ansible/roles/mtv_operator) checks it and customizes it for the class: - (demo-openshift) Namespace openshift-mtv, OperatorGroup migration (targets openshift-mtv), and Subscription mtv-operator: channel release-v2.11, source redhat-operators. CI waits for the CSV to report Succeeded. - (demo-openshift) ForkliftController/forklift-controller with feature_ui_plugin, feature_validation, feature_volume_populator and feature_must_gather_api all "true". (CI) adds controller_precopy_interval: "5" for Demo 2 and waits for deploy/forklift-controller to be Available. - (demo-openshift; CI re-checks) MTV's console plugin enabled in consoles.operator.openshift.io/cluster → spec.plugins. This is what adds the Migration for Virtualization menu. - Class access: RoleBinding ovedr-students-view (ClusterRole view) and Role + RoleBinding ovedr-students-migrate. The second lets students create, start and delete plans and migrations, and only read providers, maps and hosts. It never grants secrets.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get subscription mtv-operator -o jsonpath='{.spec.channel}{"\n"}'   # release-v2.11
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get csv | grep mtv
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get forkliftcontroller,deploy/forklift-controller
oc --context site-a get console.operator cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.plugins}{"\n"}'                    # includes forklift…
oc --context site-a auth can-i create plans.forklift.konveyor.io -n openshift-mtv                        # yes (students)

Do it yourself (CLI):

oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: { name: openshift-mtv }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata: { name: migration, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { targetNamespaces: [ openshift-mtv ] }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata: { name: mtv-operator, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { name: mtv-operator, channel: release-v2.11, source: redhat-operators, sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace }
YAML
oc -n openshift-mtv get csv -w                                  # wait for Succeeded, then:
oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: ForkliftController
metadata: { name: forklift-controller, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  feature_ui_plugin: "true"
  feature_validation: "true"
  feature_volume_populator: "true"
  feature_must_gather_api: "true"
YAML
PLUGIN=$(oc get consoleplugin -o name | grep forklift | cut -d/ -f2); echo "$PLUGIN"
oc patch console.operator cluster --type json -p "[{\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/plugins/-\",\"value\":\"$PLUGIN\"}]"

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → Migration Toolkit for Virtualization Operator → Install, channel release-v2.11, namespace openshift-mtv. 📸 S-mtv-operatorhub 2. Installed Operators → MTV → ForkliftController → Create. 📸 S-mtv-forkliftcontroller 3. Accept "Web console update is available" and refresh. Migration for Virtualization appears in the menu. 📸 S-mtv-menu

docs.title: S.6 The vSphere side: an MTV account, its role, and the vSphere provider
docs.text:
What CI built (automation/customize/mtv_fabric.sh): - On vCenter, an SSO user ovedr-mtv@vsphere.local, with a minted password stored in the class vault and never shown, and a role ovedr-mtv with MTV's minimal privilege set: - power on/off and guest control; - all of Provisioning; - create/remove snapshot; - ChangeTracking (CBT, for warm migration); - datastore browse and file management; - session validation; - Cryptographer decrypt/access.

It is granted on the vCenter root (/), propagating. CI checks the user can then list the inventory. - A network probe run from inside each cluster before any provider: vCenter 443, every ESXi host on 443 and 902 (MTV's disk copy), and the peer cluster's api-int 6443 and ingress 443. - On each tooled site, Secret + Provider/ovedr-vcenter0<N> (type vsphere, url https://vcenter0<N>…/sdk). It carries user, password, url and cacert: the certificate chain vCenter serves, so TLS is verified, never skipped. - VDDK: the step before (vddk) copies the lab's saved VDDK image into the cluster's registry, and the provider gets settings.vddkInitImage pointing at it. Without it, migrations are cold only and slower. Warm migration (Demo 2) needs it. Why the customer must supply it, and how to build it: S.15.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}  {.spec.url}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" -o jsonpath='{.spec.settings}{"\n"}'   # vddkInitImage?

Do it yourself (CLI): the vSphere role and user (govc, as a vCenter administrator), then the provider:

export GOVC_URL="https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN" GOVC_USERNAME='administrator@vsphere.local'   # GOVC_PASSWORD from your vault
govc role.create my-mtv VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn \
  VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking \
  Datastore.Browse Datastore.FileManagement Sessions.ValidateSession   # … plus Provisioning.*, GuestControl, Cryptographer.*
govc sso.user.create -p '<password>' my-mtv        # the one place a password goes on argv: govc has no other way
govc permissions.set -principal my-mtv@vsphere.local -role my-mtv -propagate=true /

CA="$(openssl s_client -showcerts -servername "vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN" -connect "vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN:443" </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
      | sed -n '/-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/,/-----END CERTIFICATE-----/p')"
oc -n openshift-mtv create secret generic my-vcenter --from-literal=user=my-mtv@vsphere.local \
  --from-literal=password='<password>' --from-literal=url="https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN/sdk" --from-literal=cacert="$CA" \
  --from-literal=insecureSkipVerify=false
oc -n openshift-mtv label secret my-vcenter createdForProviderType=vsphere createdForResourceType=providers
oc apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: my-vcenter, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { type: vsphere, url: "https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN/sdk", secret: { name: my-vcenter, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
YAML

Console: 1. vSphere Client: Administration → Roles → New (privileges as above); Single Sign On → Users and Groups → Add; Hosts and Clusters → vCenter → Permissions → Add. 📸 S-vsphere-role · 📸 S-vsphere-permission 2. OpenShift: Migration for Virtualization → Providers → Create Provider → VMware: URL, user, password, and either fetch certificate or paste the CA. 📸 S-mtv-provider-vsphere 3. The provider shows Ready, with VM and host counts. 📸 S-mtv-provider-ready

Red Hat docs: - VMware prerequisites and privileges for MTV [verify link] - Adding a VMware vSphere source provider [verify link] - Creating a VDDK image [verify link]

docs.title: S.7 OpenShift ⇄ OpenShift providers
docs.text:
What CI built: on both sites, ServiceAccount ovedr-mtv-peer in openshift-mtv (bound to cluster-admin, MTV's documented simplest grant for an OpenShift source; the cluster exists only for the booking) and a long-lived token Secret ovedr-mtv-peer-token. On each tooled site, a Provider ovedr-ocp-<peer> (type openshift) whose url and cacert both come from the peer's kubeconfig: the URL is https://api-int.<peer>…:6443 and the CA is the cluster's internal CA.

💡 Why api-int and not api? After demo-openshift's customize, api.<cluster> serves a public Let's Encrypt certificate. api-int keeps the cluster's internal CA. URL and CA must come from the same place, or TLS verification fails (x509: certificate signed by unknown authority). That happened in this lab, and it is why CI reads both from one kubeconfig.

Check:

oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-ocp-${A#ocp-}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}  {.spec.url}{"\n"}'

Do it yourself (CLI): on the source cluster, create the service account and token. On the destination, create the provider.

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv create sa my-peer
oc --context site-a adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin -z my-peer -n openshift-mtv
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
metadata: { name: my-peer-token, namespace: openshift-mtv, annotations: { kubernetes.io/service-account.name: my-peer } }
YAML
TOKEN="$(oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get secret my-peer-token -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)"
URL="https://api-int.$A.$DOMAIN:6443"                  # match the CA below
oc --context site-a config view --raw --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d > peer-ca.pem
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv create secret generic my-ocp-a --from-literal=token="$TOKEN" \
  --from-literal=url="$URL" --from-file=cacert=peer-ca.pem --from-literal=insecureSkipVerify=false
oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv label secret my-ocp-a createdForProviderType=openshift createdForResourceType=providers
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: my-ocp-a, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { type: openshift, url: "$URL", secret: { name: my-ocp-a, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
YAML
unset TOKEN; rm -f peer-ca.pem

Console: site B, Migration for Virtualization → Providers → Create Provider → OpenShift Virtualization: URL, service-account token, CA certificate. 📸 S-mtv-provider-ocp

Red Hat docs: - Adding an OpenShift Virtualization source provider [verify link] - Using service accounts [verify link]

docs.title: S.8 Network maps and storage maps
docs.text:
What CI built, per tooled site, in openshift-mtv:

Map Source → destination Why ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net vSphere vm-network → pod network works everywhere; the VM gets a new, cluster-internal address ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge vSphere vm-network → multus default/vmnet<22+N> the VM stays on its VLAN and keeps its own address. Created only when the NAD's bridge is Available ovedr-vcenter0<N>-storage datastore coresan01_data00 → this site's class site A: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization; site B: nfs-csi ovedr-ocp-<peer>-net pod → pod, plus each VLAN NAD present on both sites → the same NAD OVE ⇄ OVE ovedr-ocp-<peer>-storage the peer's class → this site's class OVE ⇄ OVE converts ODF ⇄ NFS: the disks are copied into the destination's storage

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get networkmap,storagemap
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get storagemap "ovedr-vcenter0$N-storage" -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}{"\n"}' | jq .

Do it yourself (CLI):

P="ovedr-vcenter0$N"
oc --context site-a apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: NetworkMap
metadata: { name: my-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  provider: { source: { name: $P, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map: [ { source: { name: vm-network }, destination: { type: multus, name: vmnet${VLAN}, namespace: default } } ]
---
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageMap
metadata: { name: my-storage, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  provider: { source: { name: $P, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map: [ { source: { name: coresan01_data00 }, destination: { storageClass: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization } } ]
YAML

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Network maps → Create (source network → Multus: default/vmnet); Storage maps → Create (datastore → storage class). 📸 S-networkmap · 📸 S-storagemap

Red Hat docs: - Creating network and storage mappings [verify link: the mappings chapter] - Migration Toolkit for Virtualization 2.11 documentation

docs.title: S.9 Namespaces: one per student (admin), plus the class namespace ovedr-app (both sites)
docs.text:
What CI built (ansible/roles/class_namespace) on both sites: - One namespace per student, named exactly the student's class ID in lower case (e.g. student-01-0024-006, the same name as their vCenter folder vms/students/<class ID>). Their VM migrates there. - The student is admin there: full rights, scoped to that namespace only. That is one RoleBinding (ovedr-student-admin-<hash>) per identity the student can log in as: the htpasswd user (their class ID) and, with SSO, their UPN. - The instructors' group demo-instructors is admin there too (ovedr-instructors-admin). - Their VM's Service <vm>-sql (selector vm.kubevirt.io/name: <vm>, port 5432). - Their browser terminal, Deployment sql-client + ConfigMap ovedr-tools (see The browser terminal below). Instructors get one in their own namespace too, pointed at win-pg-i01. - Instructors: their own namespace (their class ID; the instructor VM win-pg-i01 lands in the first instructor's), and cluster-admin on both clusters (ClusterRoleBinding/ovedr-instructor-cluster-admin-*, one per identity), so they can help with any student, storage or operator issue. CLI: oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin <user>; console: User Management → RoleBindings → Create binding (cluster-wide, role cluster-admin). Using RBAC [verify link] - The class namespace ovedr-app: the shared sql-client. It holds RoleBinding ovedr-students-edit (ClusterRole edit, group demo-students), the instructor VM's Service win-pg-i01-sql, Secret bcdr-db (the bcdr database password, from the vault), and Deployment sql-client (registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16), the instructor's tool as the database owner (bcdr): the healthcheck reads every VM's heartbeat through it, and the instructor uses it for owner-only steps (Demo 1 Bonus B). Students never need it. - ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding ovedr-class-read: students may read NNCPs and node network states, storage classes, snapshot classes, ACM managed clusters and cluster sets, DR policies and clusters, and nodes.

Check:

for s in site-a site-b; do
  oc --context $s get project "$VMNS"                                     # your namespace exists on both sites
  oc --context $s -n "$VMNS" get rolebinding,svc                          # your admin binding(s) and your VM's Service
  oc --context $s -n "$VMNS" get deploy/sql-client cm/ovedr-tools           # your browser terminal and its commands
done
oc --context site-a auth can-i '*' '*' -n "$VMNS"                         # yes: admin in your own namespace
oc --context site-a auth can-i create pods/exec -n "$VMNS"                  # yes: the console's Terminal tab needs it
oc --context site-a auth can-i list nodenetworkconfigurationpolicies      # yes (class read)

Do it yourself (CLI): a namespace for a student with admin rights, and the VM's Service:

NS=student-99-demo                         # a student's namespace = their class ID, lower case
U=student-99-demo                          # the user they log in as (add a second binding for their SSO UPN)
oc new-project "$NS" --display-name="$U: your VM migrates here"
oc adm policy add-role-to-user admin "$U" -n "$NS"                        # full rights, only in this namespace
oc adm policy add-role-to-group admin demo-instructors -n "$NS"           # instructors too
oc -n "$NS" create service clusterip "$VM-sql" --tcp=5432:5432 --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | sed "s/app: $VM-sql/vm.kubevirt.io\/name: $VM/" | oc apply -f -

The class namespace, by hand:

oc new-project my-app
oc -n my-app create rolebinding students-edit --clusterrole=edit --group=demo-students
oc -n my-app create secret generic bcdr-db --from-literal=PGPASSWORD='<bcdr password>'
oc -n my-app create deployment sql-client --image=registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16 -- sleep infinity
oc -n my-app set env deployment/sql-client --from=secret/bcdr-db

Console: 1. Home → Projects → Create Project: the name is the student's class ID. 📸 S-namespace 2. That project → Project access (or User Management → RoleBindings → Create binding): subject User = the student, role admin; add the group demo-instructors as admin. 📸 S-project-access 3. Networking → Services → Create Service in that project (selector vm.kubevirt.io/name). 📸 S-service 4. In ovedr-app: Workloads → Secrets → Create and Workloads → Deployments → Create for sql-client.

docs.title: The browser terminal (one per student and instructor, both sites)
docs.text:
The class runs entirely in the browser (operator, 2026-10-12): students are external, may not install anything on their computers, and have no network path to the lab. So every command runs in a pod of their own, opened from the console's Terminal tab (the console's exec, which admin in their namespace allows).

What CI built, in every student's and instructor's namespace (ansible/roles/class_namespace): - ConfigMap ovedr-tools: the class commands (dblogin, mark, load, verify, alive, sql, oclogin, where, ovedr), mounted at /opt/ovedr/bin (mode 0755). Source: ansible/roles/class_namespace/files/ovedr-tools/. - Deployment sql-client (rhel9/postgresql-16, sleep infinity), with: - init containers that copy oc from the cluster's own openshift/cli image, fetch virtctl from OpenShift Virtualization's in-cluster download service, and fetch jq (pinned, checksum-verified); - its environment preset per person: ME, VM, VM_IP, VMNS, WINUSER, N, A, B, VC, SITE, and PGHOST (the VM's own address), PGUSER (student_NN), PGDATABASE=bcdr; - no password anywhere: dblogin asks for the student's class password once and keeps it in the pod (~/.pgpass, 0600); oclogin takes the token from the console's Copy login command, so oc and virtctl act as the student. The pod has no service-account token (automountServiceAccountToken: false). - A change to the commands rolls the pod (annotation ovedr/tools-sha). The healthcheck drives student-01's terminal on both sites, as the student: dblogin, alive, verify, and oc/virtctl/jq present.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get deploy/sql-client -o jsonpath='{.status.availableReplicas}{"\n"}'   # 1
ovedr                                                                    # in the Terminal: who, where, what is signed in

Do it yourself (CLI): the same idea for any namespace (here without the class commands):

oc -n "$NS" create deployment toolbox --image=registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16 -- sleep infinity
oc -n "$NS" set env deployment/toolbox PGHOST=<VM address> PGUSER=<login> PGDATABASE=bcdr

Console: Workloads → Pods → sql-client-… → Terminal. 📸 S-browser-terminal

Red Hat docs: - Working with projects [verify link] - Using RBAC to define and apply permissions [verify link] - Default cluster roles (admin, edit, view) [verify link] - Exposing a VM by using a Service [verify link]

docs.title: S.10 Demo preparation
docs.text:
What CI built (demo-prep job, ansible/roles/demo_prep and the play after it): - MTV pre-copy interval: ForkliftController.spec.controller_precopy_interval: 5 (minutes), so a warm migration (Demo 2) shows several pre-copies instead of one per hour [verify: field name on MTV 2.11]. - Snapshot classes: see S.4. - ACM: if site B is an ACM hub and site A is not, CI creates a ManagedCluster for site A with an auto-import-secret (site A's kubeconfig; ACM deletes it after use) and waits for Available. ⚠ demo-openshift now installs ACM on both clusters. A cluster that is itself a hub cannot simply be imported into another hub, so CI skips the import and the readiness table says so (BL-D11, an open decision). - A per-demo readiness table in the run summary: which demos this booking can run (for example, Demo 2 needs a VDDK image).

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get forkliftcontroller forklift-controller -o jsonpath='{.spec}{"\n"}' | jq .
oc --context site-b get managedclusters                       # local-cluster, and site A if imported

Do it yourself (CLI):

oc -n openshift-mtv patch forkliftcontroller forklift-controller --type merge -p '{"spec":{"controller_precopy_interval":5}}'
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: ManagedCluster
metadata: { name: $A, labels: { cloud: auto-detect, vendor: auto-detect } }
spec: { hubAcceptsClient: true }
YAML
# then, in namespace $A on the hub: Secret auto-import-secret with autoImportRetry and site A's kubeconfig (or token + server)

docs.title: S.11 The class VMs on vSphere
docs.text:
What CI built (source_vm.sh, student_vms.sh, lib/vm.sh, windows/*.ps1), entirely through vCenter's API (govc) and VMware guest operations: - Instructor VM win-pg-i01 in vms/ovedr: Windows Server 2022 (BIOS, LSI Logic SAS, e1000e), installed unattended from the lab ISO plus an answer ISO (VMware Tools included). Three disks: C: 60 GB, L: 5 GB (PostgreSQL WAL, label pg_wal) and D: 10 GB (PostgreSQL data, label pgdata). Static address 10.101.<22+N>.62. - PostgreSQL 16 runs as service postgresql-16, with PGDATA=D:\pgdata and WAL at L:\pg_wal. - The bcdr database holds the heartbeat writer (a startup task) and the integrity toolkit (ovedr_mark/load/verify/checksum). - Each roster account has a Windows login (.\student-NN). - WinRM is enabled over HTTPS (5986, lab networks only) so Ansible can manage the VM. - One VM per student, win-pg-s<NN>: a full clone of the instructor VM's snapshot ovedr-golden, 2 vCPU / 4 GB. - Re-addressed to 10.101.<22+N>.<100+NN> with its network card disconnected, so it never appears with the instructor's address. - Renamed, with its own WinRM certificate. Its student is a local administrator. - Moved into vms/students/<your ID>, where you hold vCenter rights on it (role ovedr-student-vm: power, console, Edit Settings, snapshots). - Every VM is validated in the guest before you get it (Test-SourceVm.ps1: volumes, the PostgreSQL layout, the heartbeat, the toolkit, logins, the address, WinRM). - On the shared datastore every VM's folder carries its zone (ovedr-<zone>-<name>), so classes on different zones never collide.

Check:

alive; verify                                                # toolkit commands: your VM answers and your chain is intact

In vCenter: VMs and Templates → datacenter01 → vm → vms → students → → win-pg-s<NN> → Summary, Configure → Hardware (three disks). 📸 S-vm-in-student-folder · 📸 S-vm-disks

Do it yourself (CLI, condensed from the CI scripts):

export GOVC_URL="https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN"                 # credentials from your vault
F=/datacenter01/vm/vms/ovedr; POOL="/datacenter01/host/cluster-lz$N/Resources"; DS=coresan01_data00
govc vm.create -on=false -folder "$F" -pool "$POOL" -ds "$DS" -c 4 -m 8192 -g windows2019srvNext_64Guest \
  -firmware bios -net vm-network -net.adapter e1000e -disk.controller lsilogic-sas -disk 60GB \
  -iso '<path of the Windows ISO>' -iso-datastore "$DS" my-win-pg
govc vm.disk.create -vm my-win-pg -ds "$DS" -name my-win-pg/log  -size 5GB
govc vm.disk.create -vm my-win-pg -ds "$DS" -name my-win-pg/data -size 10GB
# … install Windows + PostgreSQL (initdb -D D:\pgdata -X L:\pg_wal), then clone one per student:
govc snapshot.create -vm my-win-pg -m=false golden
govc vm.clone -vm my-win-pg -snapshot golden -link=false -on=false -folder "$F" -pool "$POOL" -ds "$DS" -c 2 -m 4096 my-win-pg-s01

docs.text:
What CI built (automation/customize/stage.sh), for every class VM (win-pg-i01 and every win-pg-s<NN>):

Site Plan Moves site A d1-<vm> vSphere → site A, cold (Demo 1) site A d2-<vm> vSphere → site A, warm (Demo 2): lands as <vm>-warm. It waits on Changed Block Tracking, which the student enables in Demo 2 (staged and reported, never blocking) site B d1b-<vm>-to-<B slot> vSphere → site B, cold (Demo 1b) site B d2b-<vm>-to-<B slot> vSphere → site B, warm: lands as <vm>-warm, waits on CBT like d2-<vm>

docs.title: S.14 How the two clusters are joined: ACM, Submariner, then ODF disaster recovery
docs.text:
Two clusters become one DR pair in three layers, and each layer needs the one before it. Demo 3 (moving a VM between clusters) needs only MTV's providers (S.7). Demo 4 (ODF Regional-DR) needs all three layers.

  layer 1  ACM       one hub MANAGES both clusters        ManagedCluster, ManagedClusterSet
  layer 2  Submariner the clusters' pod/service networks  submariner add-on, Broker, (Globalnet)
           can reach each other
  layer 3  ODF DR    Ceph RBD mirroring between the two   ODF Multicluster Orchestrator: MirrorPeer,
           ODF clusters, driven from the hub              DRCluster, DRPolicy; per app: DRPlacementControl

docs.title: What this lab has today (read live on 0024-008, 2026-10-08)
docs.text:
ocp-lzX (site A) ocp-lzY (site B) ACM MultiClusterHub 2.16.6, its own hub (manages only local-cluster) the same: its own hub Joined to the other? no no Submariner add-on available on the hub, not deployed available, not deployed ODF ODF 4.19 (ocs-storagecluster Ready, 4 scratch SSDs) none: NFS only (the lab has SSDs for one ODF site) Pod / service networks 10.128.0.0/14 / 172.30.0.0/16 the same: overlapping, so Submariner needs Globalnet

That was before acm_join.sh: on 0024-008 the clusters were not joined. From the next deploy, CI joins them on every deploy (layer 1 below). ODF replication (layer 3) also needs ODF on both sites, which waits on more SSDs.

docs.title: Layer 1: one hub manages both clusters (ACM)
docs.text:
Automated on every deploy: CI's demo-prep job runs automation/customize/acm_join.sh. The commands below are what it does, so you can do the same by hand.

Design for this lab: site B is the hub, and site A is imported into it as a managed cluster. Site B's own local-cluster is the second managed cluster. Because site A also runs a hub, its self-management must be turned off first [verify: importing a cluster that runs a MultiClusterHub into another hub, ACM 2.16; the supported alternative is Multicluster Global Hub]. That is a change to how demo-openshift built site A's ACM, so it waits on their agreement (BL-D11).

CLI (instructor; on the hub site-b unless noted):

A_NAME="ocp-$A"
# 1. site A's hub does not manage itself: done at BUILD time by demo-openshift's member option acm=managed (this
#    demo books site A that way). By hand on a standalone cluster it is this one field:
#    oc --context site-a patch mch multiclusterhub -n open-cluster-management --type merge -p '{"spec":{"disableHubSelfManagement":true}}'
oc --context site-a get mch -A -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.disableHubSelfManagement}{"\n"}'      # true
# 2. on the hub: a namespace + ManagedCluster for site A, and a one-time auto-import secret with site A's kubeconfig
oc --context site-b create namespace "$A_NAME" --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc --context site-b apply -f -
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: ManagedCluster
metadata: { name: $A_NAME, labels: { cloud: auto-detect, vendor: auto-detect, cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset: ovedr } }
spec: { hubAcceptsClient: true }
EOF
oc --context site-b -n "$A_NAME" create secret generic auto-import-secret \
  --from-literal=autoImportRetry=5 --from-file=kubeconfig="$HOME/.kube/site-a.kubeconfig"   # ACM deletes it after import
# 3. a cluster set holding both clusters (DR policies select clusters by set)
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSet
metadata: { name: ovedr }
EOF
oc --context site-b label managedcluster local-cluster cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset=ovedr --overwrite
oc --context site-b get managedclusters          # local-cluster and ocp-<A>: JOINED True, AVAILABLE True

Console: site B → All Clusters (top-left switcher) → Infrastructure → Clusters → Import cluster: name ocp-<A>, cluster set ovedr, import mode Kubeconfig (paste site A's), Import. Then Cluster sets → Create cluster set ovedr and add both clusters. 📸 S-acm-import · 📸 S-acm-clusters. Red Hat: Importing a managed cluster [verify link] · Managed cluster sets [verify link].

docs.title: Layer 2: the clusters' networks reach each other (Submariner)
docs.text:
ODF mirrors Ceph images over the clusters' pod/service networks. Here both clusters use the same CIDRs, so Submariner runs with Globalnet, which gives each cluster a non-overlapping virtual range.

Console: hub → Infrastructure → Clusters → Cluster sets → ovedr → Submariner add-ons → Install Submariner add-ons, select both clusters, enable Globalnet, keep the defaults, Install. Wait until both show Healthy (connection and agent). 📸 S-submariner-install · 📸 S-submariner-healthy.

CLI (the add-on is a ManagedClusterAddOn per cluster plus a broker in the set's namespace) [verify: field names, ACM 2.16]:

oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: submariner.io/v1alpha1
kind: Broker
metadata: { name: submariner-broker, namespace: ovedr-broker }
spec: { globalnetEnabled: true }
EOF
for c in local-cluster "ocp-$A"; do
  oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: addon.open-cluster-management.io/v1alpha1
kind: ManagedClusterAddOn
metadata: { name: submariner, namespace: $c }
spec: { installNamespace: submariner-operator }
EOF
done
oc --context site-b get managedclusteraddon -A | grep submariner     # AVAILABLE True on both

docs.title: Layer 3: linking ODF for replication (Demo 4)
docs.text:
Each site runs its own Ceph cluster (ODF). Replication links the two so every protected RBD image (a VM disk) on the primary is mirrored to the other site as snapshots on a schedule. The link has four parts, all created from the hub:

Part What it is Created by MCG (NooBaa) on both sites object storage where Ramen keeps each protected app's DR metadata dr_fabric.sh step 1 (ODF ships it off here) MirrorPeer pairs the two StorageClusters: exchanges Ceph keys/endpoints, turns on RBD mirroring (rbd-mirror daemons) between them, over Submariner dr_fabric.sh step 3 (or the console's DRPolicy wizard) DRCluster × 2 the hub's view of each site as a DR peer (its S3 profile, fencing state) ODF Multicluster Orchestrator, from the MirrorPeer DRPolicy "these two clusters, async, every 15m" dr_policy.sh (<A>-<B>-15m)

Then each protected application (Demo 4: the ovedr-app + student namespaces) gets a DRPlacementControl on the hub, which tells Ramen which cluster is primary and drives Failover/Relocate.

Prerequisites, in order: both clusters managed by the hub (layer 1) · Submariner connected (layer 2) · ODF Ready on both sites · then the parts above.

CLI (hub = site B; what dr_fabric.sh / dr_policy.sh apply) [verify on first ODF-on-both booking]:

A_NAME="ocp-$A"; B_NAME=local-cluster
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: multicluster.odf.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: MirrorPeer
metadata: { name: ovedr-$A-$B }
spec:
  type: async
  manageS3: true
  schedulingIntervals: [ 2m, 5m, 15m ]
  items:
    - { clusterName: $A_NAME, storageClusterRef: { name: ocs-storagecluster, namespace: openshift-storage } }
    - { clusterName: $B_NAME, storageClusterRef: { name: ocs-storagecluster, namespace: openshift-storage } }
EOF
oc --context site-b get mirrorpeer,drcluster                                       # DRClusters Validated=True
oc --context site-b apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: ramendr.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: DRPolicy
metadata: { name: ocp-$A-ocp-$B-15m }
spec: { drClusters: [ $A_NAME, $B_NAME ], schedulingInterval: 15m }
EOF
oc --context site-b get drpolicy -o wide                                          # Validated=True
# the link itself, seen from each Ceph cluster (instructor: rook-ceph-tools)
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools rbd mirror pool status ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool

Console: hub → All Clusters → Data Services → Disaster recovery → Create DRPolicy: select both clusters, replication Asynchronous, interval 15m, Create. The wizard creates the MirrorPeer and DRClusters for you. 📸 S-drpolicy-create · 📸 S-drpolicy-validated.

Requires ODF on both sites, which waits on more scratch SSDs (BL-C20). CI runs dr-fabric and dr-policy when a booking sets DR=on. Red Hat: ODF Regional-DR [verify link].

docs.title: S.15 VDDK: the one piece the customer supplies (Broadcom licence)
docs.text:
What it is. The VMware Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK) is VMware's library for reading a VM's disks straight from ESXi. MTV uses it to copy disks, and for a warm migration to copy only the blocks that changed since the last pass (VMware's Changed Block Tracking, Demo 2). Warm migration needs it; a cold migration works without it, only slower [verify: MTV 2.11 cold path without VDDK].

Why you supply it. VDDK is Broadcom's software, and its licence does not allow Red Hat, Paragon Micro or anyone else to redistribute it. So OpenShift doesn't ship it, and neither does this lab's code: each customer downloads VDDK themselves from Broadcom's developer portal with their own account, accepts the licence, builds a small container image from it, and keeps that image in their own private registry. Never put the tarball or the image in git or a public registry. In a real migration project this is one of the first prerequisites to arrange.

How to build it (Red Hat's procedure):

  1. Download VDDK 8.0.x for Linux (VMware-vix-disklib-<version>.x86_64.tar.gz) from Broadcom's developer portal.
  2. Unpack it next to this Containerfile:
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8/ubi-minimal
USER 1001
COPY vmware-vix-disklib-distrib /vmware-vix-disklib-distrib
RUN mkdir -p /opt
ENTRYPOINT ["cp", "-r", "/vmware-vix-disklib-distrib", "/opt"]
  1. Build and push it to a private registry. On OpenShift, the cluster's own registry works, with no tool on your laptop:
tar -xzf VMware-vix-disklib-*.x86_64.tar.gz                  # → vmware-vix-disklib-distrib/
oc -n openshift-mtv new-build --name vddk --binary --strategy docker
oc -n openshift-mtv start-build vddk --from-dir=. --follow   # the directory with the Containerfile and the unpacked kit
oc -n openshift-mtv get istag vddk:latest                    # image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/openshift-mtv/vddk:latest

MTV's migration pods run in the target namespace, so let every service account pull from openshift-mtv:

oc -n openshift-mtv policy add-role-to-group system:image-puller system:serviceaccounts
  1. Point the vSphere provider at it. Console: Migration for Virtualization → Providers → your vSphere provider → VDDK init image → edit. CLI:
oc -n openshift-mtv patch provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"settings":{"vddkInitImage":"image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/openshift-mtv/vddk:latest"}}}'

How this lab does it (automation/customize/vddk.sh, job vddk, after MTV is installed):

  1. Once per VDDK version, the operator downloads the kit with the lab's Broadcom account and runs automation/tools/vddk_image.sh <kit>. It builds the image above and saves it in the lab's private registry (never git, never public: the script refuses to finish if the image can be read without credentials). The image holds the unpacked kit, so it is also the lab's only stored copy of the download.
  2. Every booking, on each cluster that runs MTV: a Docker BuildConfig whose Containerfile is just FROM <the saved image> copies it into the cluster's own registry as openshift-mtv/vddk:<version>, with a short-lived read-only pull credential that is deleted when the build ends. Then the image-puller grant above.
  3. The vSphere provider gets vddkInitImage: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/openshift-mtv/vddk:<version>, and the run's readiness table shows Demo 2 ready.

So nothing is redistributed, the licensed file leaves the lab's private storage only into the lab's own clusters, and a booking never waits on a download. If no saved image exists yet, the vddk job warns, Demo 2 shows blocked and the warm plans show VDDKInitImageUnavailable (Demo 2 §2.5); the cold class runs as normal.

Where Broadcom keeps it: VDDK moved to Broadcom's developer portal (developer.broadcom.com → SDKs → VMware Virtual Disk Development Kit), behind a Broadcom sign-in. Older VMware download links no longer work. Use a VDDK version your vSphere release and your MTV release both support (Red Hat's MTV prerequisites list them).

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" -o jsonpath='{.spec.settings.vddkInitImage}{"\n"}'   # the image
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get plan -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  "}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="VDDKInitImageUnavailable")].status}{"\n"}{end}'   # empty: no plan lacks it

docs.text:
Version 0.2.0 · draft · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/toolkit.md

The reference every demo uses. Lab 0 signs you in and opens a command line; this page has the rest: your class terminal on both sites, the commands that write and prove your data, your file in the VM, and the proof table. Each demo points at the section it needs.

docs.title: T.1 Your class terminal, signed in on both sites
docs.text: 🎬 T.1 Your class terminal, signed in on both sites: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/toolkit-t-1-class-terminal-both-sites.mp4).

docs.title: Open it
docs.text:
Every command in these guides runs in your browser terminal: a shell inside your own pod, sql-client, opened from the OpenShift console. Nothing is installed on your computer. It has psql, the class commands (T.2), oc, virtctl and jq, and it already knows who you are and where your VM is. You have one on each site; use the one on site A unless a guide says otherwise.

  1. In the site A console, open your project: Home → Projects → <your class ID> (or pick it in the Project list at the top of any page).
  2. Go to Workloads → Pods, open the pod sql-client-…, and choose the Terminal tab.
  3. Type ovedr and press Enter. It shows your class ID, your VM and its address, which site this terminal is on, and what is signed in yet.

📋 Copy and paste. The Terminal tab is a normal browser terminal: - Paste a command from these guides with right-click → Paste, or Ctrl+Shift+V (Windows/Linux) / ⌘V (Mac). The copy button on each command block in the class site copies it for you. - Copy output by selecting it with the mouse, then right-click → Copy (or Ctrl+Shift+C / ⌘C). Plain Ctrl+C stops the running command, as in any terminal. - Paste one block at a time and wait for the prompt. Most class commands are one short line you can also type.

[verify: paste and copy shortcuts in the 4.19 console terminal, per browser]

💡 The terminal keeps your sign-ins while the pod runs, even if you close the tab or the browser. If the pod is ever restarted, run dblogin and oclogin again. Leaving a long command running? Keep its tab open.

docs.title: Sign its oc in, for both sites
docs.text:
With SSO, oc signs in with a token from the console, never a password. Do this once per site, in the same terminal:

  1. In the site A console, open your name (top right) → Copy login command → Display Token. Copy the line that starts with oc login --token=….
  2. In your terminal, type oclogin and a space, paste the line, and press Enter.
  3. Repeat in the site B console: copy its login command and paste it after oclogin in the same terminal.
oclogin oc login --token=sha256~… --server=https://api.ocp-lz1.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com:6443   # ✓ site-a: signed in as …
oclogin oc login --token=sha256~… --server=https://api.ocp-lz2.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com:6443   # ✓ site-b: signed in as …

oclogin names each sign-in after its site, so every later command says which cluster it talks to (--context site-a / --context site-b), and it sets your namespace as the default. Tokens last 24 hours: if oc says Unauthorized, repeat the step for that site.

oc --context site-a whoami && oc --context site-b whoami   # both print your class ID
oc --context site-a get project "$VMNS"                    # yours, on site A …
oc --context site-b get project "$VMNS"                    # … and on site B
oc --context site-a auth can-i '*' '*' -n "$VMNS"          # yes: admin in your own namespace

docs.title: What it already knows
docs.text:
⚠️ The landing zones change from booking to booking. The scheduler picks whichever zones are free, so your vSphere zone can be lz1, lz2 or lz3, and your two clusters any two of ocp-lz1, ocp-lz2, ocp-lz3, in any order (for example vSphere lz2 with site A ocp-lz3 and site B ocp-lz1). The examples in these guides use lz1 / ocp-lz1 / ocp-lz2. Always use your booking's values (the instructor gives them out), never the examples.

Value Example ME: your class ID student-03-0024-005 N: vSphere landing zone number 1 (→ vcenter01) A: site A cluster ocp-lz1 B: site B cluster ocp-lz2

Your VM name and its vSphere address follow from your ID:

You are VM ($VM) Address on vSphere ($VM_IP) student-NN-… win-pg-sNN (e.g. student-03 → win-pg-s03) 10.101.<22+N>.<100+NN> (e.g. 10.101.23.103) the instructor win-pg-i01 (the instructor's VM, in vms/ovedr) 10.101.<22+N>.62

[verify: BL-D10, per-student clones and their address plan]

You don't type these in. Your browser terminal (T.1) already holds all of them, and your VM's name and address, as $ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $VMNS, $WINUSER, $VC and $DOMAIN. Type ovedr there to see them.

Your namespace, $VMNS. On both OpenShift clusters you have your own namespace (project), named exactly your class ID in lower case, for example student-03-0024-005. It matches your vCenter folder. You are admin there: full rights, scoped to that namespace only. Your migration plans land your VM there, and your VM's SQL Service ($VM-sql) lives there, and so does your browser terminal, pod sql-client (T.1). Instructors get their own namespace too (their class ID, where win-pg-i01 lands), are admin in every student namespace, and are cluster-admin on both clusters, so they can help with any student, storage or operator issue.

docs.title: T.2 The data-integrity commands
docs.text:
🎬 T.2 The data-integrity commands: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/toolkit-t-2-data-integrity-commands.mp4).

The database bcdr has two tables you will use:

Table Written by What it proves heartbeat a writer in the VM, every 5 s the VM is alive. Gaps in it are outages. marks you, at every stage your data survived every move, unchanged and in order

Each of your marks rows carries a SHA-256 hash of the previous row. If a row is lost, changed or reordered, ovedr_verify reports chain_ok = f and names the first broken row.

docs.title: Your class commands (already in your terminal)
docs.text:
Command What it does dblogin sign in to your VM's database as you (student_NN), with your class password. Once per pod mark <label> [note] inject one hash-chained row; note its id. Example: mark d1-before load <label> [rows] inject a burst of rows (default 100) verify read and prove your rows: chain_ok = t, and the fingerprint of all marks alive is your VM writing? staleness under 10 s = yes sql [psql options] psql to your VM's database, e.g. sql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM marks" where which site and node runs your VM right now tools after a migration: VMware Tools out, the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent in (your VM's own report) ovedr who and where you are, and what is signed in

They talk to your VM at its own address, $VM_IP, which it keeps on vSphere, site A and site B (the staged plans use a bridge network map). So they work from either site's terminal, before and after every move. If you ever move your VM onto the pod network yourself, T.4 shows how to point them at its new address (export PGHOST=…).

dblogin                          # Password for student_NN: your class password (it is not shown as you type)

ovedr_checksum fingerprints every mark in your VM's database. On your own VM that is your rows only. On the instructor's win-pg-i01 it covers everyone who marked it.

docs.title: Try it now
docs.text:
alive                            # staleness under 10 s: your VM is writing
mark first-row                  # your first row: note its id and sha
verify                           # chain_ok = t, marks = 1

📸 toolkit-verify: the verify output with chain_ok = t.

✍️ Proof table, row 0 (at the start of Demo 1): your first mark's id, and the fingerprint from ovedr_checksum.

💡 Why a hash chain? A count can't tell you that row 7 was replaced, or that rows 7 and 8 swapped places. A chain can. A migration or a failover that loses, rewrites or reorders even one of your rows shows up here as chain_ok = f.

docs.title: T.3 Your Windows VM, and your file in it
docs.text:
🎬 T.3 Your Windows VM, and your file in it: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/toolkit-t-3-windows-vm-file.mp4).

Your VM runs Windows Server 2022 with PostgreSQL 16. The WAL (write-ahead log) is on L: (5 GB) and the data is on D: (10 GB).

  • While it is on vSphere: in vCenter, select your VM and choose Launch Web Console.
  • Once it is on OpenShift: in the console, go to Virtualization → VirtualMachines → your VM → Console.

Send Ctrl-Alt-Del from the console toolbar, then log in as .\<WINUSER> (for example .\student-03) with your class password [verify: BL-D08, student Windows accounts].

docs.title: Your file in the VM
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in the VM and leave your mark on disk, not just in the database:

$f = "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force (Split-Path $f) | Out-Null
Add-Content $f "$(Get-Date -Format o)  first-row"
Get-Content $f

Every demo adds a line to this file at each stage. Its last step reads the file back on the target platform.

docs.title: T.4 (Optional) Give your VM a pod-network address on OpenShift
docs.text:
🎬 T.4 (Optional) Give your VM a pod-network address on OpenShift: a recording of this whole section, done in the console (placeholder until recorded: class/.images/toolkit-t-4-optional-pod-network-address.mp4).

You usually skip this. Every class VM has its own static address (instructor .62, students .100+NN), and the staged migration plans use the bridge network map (ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net-bridge), which puts the migrated NIC on the same VLAN. So after a move your VM answers at the same $VM_IP as before, and every helper keeps working.

Do this step only when your VM landed on the pod network: a plan you built yourself with the pod map (ovedr-vcenter0<N>-net), or a site without the bridge. A Windows static address on a pod-network NIC answers nothing, so you swap it for a pod NIC that gets its address by DHCP, and then test over that address.

ℹ️ Demo-only, not a production pattern. Swapping the NIC is a lab workaround for a VM that landed on the pod network. In a real migration the VM keeps its own NIC, MAC and address (a bridge map onto the same VLAN, as the staged plans do, or a planned re-IP), and nobody swaps NICs. Proper per-VM addressing (DHCP on the lab VLANs) is on the backlog (BL-D12). Background: Virtual machine networking [verify link].

CTX is the site your VM is now on (site-a after demos 1-2, site-b after demo 3).

docs.title: 1. Stop the VM
docs.text:
CTX=site-a
virtctl --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" stop "$VM" 2>/dev/null \
  || oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'
oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -w            # Ctrl-C at Stopped

docs.title: 2. See the migrated interface(s)
docs.text:
oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -o json \
  | jq -r '.spec.template.spec.domain.devices.interfaces as $i | .spec.template.spec.networks as $n
           | range(0; $i|length) as $k | "\($k)  \($i[$k].name)  mac=\($i[$k].macAddress // "-")  net=\($n | map(select(.name == $i[$k].name))[0] | (.pod // .multus) | tostring)"'

✍️ The index (0, 1, …) of the migrated NIC: ____

docs.title: 3. Set the migrated NIC's link down, and add a pod-network NIC
docs.text:
Console: VM → Configuration → Network → ⋮ on the migrated NIC → Set link down (or Delete), then Add network interface: network Pod networking, type Masquerade.

CLI:

IDX=0                                    # ← the index you wrote down
oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type json -p "[
 {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/interfaces/$IDX/state\",\"value\":\"down\"},
 {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/interfaces/-\",
  \"value\":{\"name\":\"default\",\"masquerade\":{},\"model\":\"virtio\"}},
 {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/networks/-\",
  \"value\":{\"name\":\"default\",\"pod\":{}}}]"

[verify: interface state: down (link state) on OpenShift Virtualization 4.19]. If your cluster rejects state, remove the migrated NIC instead: oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type json -p "[{\"op\":\"remove\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/interfaces/$IDX\"}]", then remove the matching entry under /spec/template/spec/networks/ the same way.

If the migrated NIC is already named default on the pod network (the …-net map), it is the same kind of NIC and is already unique per VM. Skip step 3 and go to step 4.

docs.title: 4. Start the VM and confirm DHCP inside Windows
docs.text:
virtctl --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" start "$VM" 2>/dev/null \
  || oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" patch vm "$VM" --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Always"}}'
oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" -w           # Ctrl-C at Running

In the VM console (.\<WINUSER>):

Get-NetAdapter | Format-Table Name, Status, MacAddress, LinkSpeed
ipconfig /all | Select-String 'Description|Physical|DHCP Enabled|IPv4|Default Gateway'

✅ The new adapter shows DHCP Enabled: Yes, and an address from OpenShift's masquerade network (the guest side is 10.0.2.2 [verify]).

The old static IP was configured on the old adapter, so the new adapter starts clean on DHCP. If Windows has pinned the static IP to the new adapter, reset it: Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias '<new adapter>' -Dhcp Enabled; ipconfig /renew.

docs.title: 5. Read your VM's address, and use it for every test
docs.text:
The guest's address is private to the VM. From outside, your VM is reached at its pod IP:

export PGHOST=$(oc --context "$CTX" -n "$VMNS" get vmi "$VM" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.interfaces[?(@.name=="default")].ipAddress}')
echo "PGHOST=$PGHOST"                    # your VM's own address on $CTX

The alternative is your VM's Service, Service/$VM-sql. It selects vm.kubevirt.io/name=$VM on port 5432, so it follows your VM whatever its IP: export PGHOST=$VM-sql.

docs.title: 6. Connection test
docs.text:
pg_isready -h "$PGHOST" -p 5432          # accepting connections
alive
mark own-address "ip=$PGHOST"
verify

✅ pg_isready answers accepting connections, the heartbeat is fresh, and chain_ok = t.

Windows has no SSH server by default, so the PostgreSQL connection above is the connection test. To work inside Windows, use the VM's Console tab in the OpenShift console.
